Regulators penalize unjustified collection and retention (C is backwards). Deleted data is gone and cannot be marketed (D).

q: Planning a 10-year archive, an architect realizes the archive will outlive two planned KMS key replacements and possibly the current vendor. Which requirement MUST be built into the archive design?
options: Only the newest key needs to be kept
Archives should store keys in the same files as data
Key continuity: every key version needed to decrypt the archive must be preserved, migratable, and documented for the archive's entire life, including vendor exit
Archive keys should be destroyed at each rotation
explain: Long archives bind key management to the retention clock (B): losing any historical key version renders that slice of the archive unreadable, so preservation and exit migration are design requirements. Destroying keys at rotation (A) or keeping only the newest (C) destroys older data. Storing keys with the data (D) defeats the encryption.

q: Producing defensible-deletion evidence for regulators, a firm wants more than an admin's assertion that a job ran. Which evidence set is MOST defensible?
options: A policy document describing deletion in general terms
A screenshot of an empty folder
Timestamped logs of the deletion workflow, the data inventory it acted on, exception and legal-hold checks, and verification sampling that the data no longer exists
An email from the cloud provider's sales team
explain: Defensible deletion is an auditable process (B): records of what was deleted, hold checks performed, and verification. A generic policy (A) proves intent, not execution. A screenshot (C) is trivially staged and unscoped. A sales email (D) carries no operational evidence.

q: Overwriting a cloud object, an engineer uploads a new version with the same name and assumes the old sensitive version is gone. With versioning enabled, what is actually true?
options: Only the bucket owner can ever delete old versions under any settings
The old version was securely wiped by the upload
Versioning encrypts old versions with a public key
The prior version is retained as a noncurrent version until lifecycle rules expire it, so deletion must explicitly address all versions
explain: Versioned buckets keep noncurrent versions (B); a put creates a new current version while the sensitive old one remains retrievable until explicitly deleted or expired by lifecycle policy. Upload does not wipe the predecessor (A). Versioning is a retention mechanism, not an encryption scheme (C). Deletion rights follow bucket policy and lock settings, not a blanket owner-only rule (D).

q: Enforcing residency for EU citizen data, a platform team needs controls that stop data landing outside approved regions in the first place, not just report it afterward. Which two controls are PREVENTIVE? (Choose two.)
options: A weekly report listing resources created in wrong regions
Organization policies or service control policies that deny resource creation in non-approved regions
A dashboard charting data location by country
Region allow-listing in the deployment pipeline so infrastructure code cannot target other regions
explain: Deny policies (A) and pipeline allow-lists (B) block non-compliant placement before it happens, which is preventive enforcement. Weekly reports (C) and dashboards (D) are detective only; they find violations after data has already landed in the wrong jurisdiction.

q: Distinguishing two requirements in a government tender, a bidder notes data will physically sit in-country, yet the provider is headquartered abroad and subject to foreign lawful-access laws. Which concept captures the remaining concern?
options: Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws and governance of the jurisdiction and operator controlling it, so physical residency alone does not remove foreign legal reach
Data classification
Data masking
Data portability
explain: Sovereignty (B) concerns which laws and authorities can compel access; a foreign-controlled operator can be ordered to produce in-country data. Classification (A) labels sensitivity. Portability (C) concerns moving data between providers. Masking (D) obscures values and does not change legal jurisdiction.

q: Passing its primary residency audit, a firm later finds its database service silently replicated backups and read replicas into a neighboring country. What is the key lesson?
options: Primary storage location is the only residency concern
Replication cannot cross borders in cloud platforms
Residency controls must cover replicas, backups, snapshots, and disaster-recovery copies, not just the primary data store
Backups are exempt from residency law in all jurisdictions
explain: Data exists wherever the platform copies it (B); residency programs that scope only primary storage miss backups, replicas, and snapshots that regulators count equally. Backups are not universally exempt (C). Cross-border replication is a common default feature, which is exactly why it must be governed (D).

q: Operating a support model for EU-hosted data, a provider warns that engineers in a third country remotely accessing the data for troubleshooting may itself breach residency commitments. Why?
options: Support engineers are exempt from data law
Residency and sovereignty commitments can be breached by cross-border access and transfer, not only by where bytes are stored
Access does not count unless data is downloaded
Remote access consumes bandwidth in the EU
explain: Many residency regimes treat remote viewing from another jurisdiction as a transfer or as foreign access (B), so support models need in-region staff, access controls, or approved transfer mechanisms. Bandwidth (A) is irrelevant. Support staff are squarely in scope (C), and screen-level access can count without any download (D).

q: Checking telemetry pipelines, a privacy engineer finds application logs, crash dumps, and support bundles containing personal data are shipped to a central analytics region overseas. What must the residency design do?
options: Classify and govern derivative data such as logs, dumps, and telemetry with the same residency rules as the source data
Encrypt logs with a key stored overseas
Delete the source database
Ignore derivatives because only the database counts
explain: Derivative data inherits the sensitivity and residency obligations of its source (B); logs and dumps are classic uncontrolled copies. Ignoring them (A) is the failure being found. Storing the decryption key overseas (C) does not fix location of the data. Deleting the source (D) does nothing for copies already shipped.

q: Adding a sovereignty control, a European bank requires its cloud encryption keys to be held in an in-country HSM under a local operator, even though storage is with a global provider. What does this control actually achieve?
options: It exempts the bank from GDPR
It moves the stored data into the country
It makes backups unnecessary
It ensures data cannot be rendered readable without an in-jurisdiction party, blunting foreign compelled access to plaintext even if ciphertext is obtained
explain: In-country key custody (B) means compelled production yields ciphertext unless the local key holder cooperates, a genuine sovereignty mitigation. It does not relocate the data itself (A). It supports but never replaces GDPR duties (C). Backup obligations are unaffected (D).

q: Releasing a health dataset, a team generalizes ZIP codes and birth dates until every combination of quasi-identifiers is shared by at least 15 people. Which property have they engineered, and what does it protect against?
options: Differential privacy, protecting query answers with noise
Tokenization, protecting card numbers in a vault
k-anonymity with k=15, protecting against singling out an individual by their combination of indirect identifiers
Encryption, protecting data at rest
explain: k-anonymity (A) requires each quasi-identifier combination to match at least k records, here 15, so no one is unique in the release. Differential privacy (B) adds calibrated noise to outputs, a different mechanism. Tokenization (C) substitutes payment values. Encryption (D) protects storage, not statistical re-identification in released data.

q: Despite k-anonymity, a released dataset lets an attacker learn every member of one small group shares the same diagnosis because that attribute lacks variety within the group. Which refinement addresses this specific flaw?
options: l-diversity, requiring each quasi-identifier group to contain a minimum diversity of sensitive values
Remove all quasi-identifiers from internal systems
Increase the password complexity for the download portal
Switch the file format to CSV
explain: The homogeneity attack defeats k-anonymity when a group's sensitive values are uniform; l-diversity (B) requires varied sensitive values per group. Portal passwords (A) control access, not inference from legitimately released data. Quasi-identifiers must stay usable in internal systems (C). File format (D) is irrelevant to inference.

q: Treating pseudonymized records as exempt, a product manager proposes dropping all GDPR safeguards for a dataset whose direct identifiers were replaced by codes. What is the CORRECT correction?
options: Codes make data impossible to re-identify under any circumstances
Pseudonymized data remains personal data under GDPR because re-identification is possible with the separately held information, so safeguards and obligations still apply
GDPR applies only to data stored on paper
Pseudonymized data is anonymous in all jurisdictions
explain: GDPR explicitly treats pseudonymized data as personal data (A) precisely because the separate mapping allows re-identification. It is anonymized data, not pseudonymized, that falls outside scope (B reverses the law). Codes with a retained mapping are re-identifiable by design (C). GDPR covers electronic processing fully (D).

q: Publishing statistics from a sensitive database, a research platform adds calibrated random noise to query answers so the presence or absence of any one person barely changes results. Which technique is this?
options: Differential privacy
Deterministic encryption
Generalization
Suppression of entire columns
explain: Differential privacy (B) bounds any individual's influence on outputs through calibrated noise, giving a mathematical privacy guarantee. Generalization (A) coarsens values in released records. Column suppression (C) removes fields outright. Deterministic encryption (D) protects stored values and leaks equality patterns, the opposite goal.

q: Claiming anonymization, a developer replaces email addresses with unsalted SHA-256 hashes and publishes the dataset. Why does this FAIL as anonymization?
options: Email addresses form a predictable space, so anyone can hash candidate emails and match them, making the hashes reversible pseudonyms rather than anonymous values
SHA-256 is too slow for datasets
Hashes are longer than email addresses
Published data can never contain hashes
explain: Deterministic hashes of predictable identifiers are dictionary-attackable (B): attackers hash known or guessed emails and re-identify rows, so this is weak pseudonymization at best. SHA-256 is fast, which is part of the problem (A is backwards). Length (C) is irrelevant. Hashes appear in published data legitimately for integrity, just not as anonymization (D).

q: Linking a supposedly anonymous survey release with a public voter roll, a journalist re-identifies respondents by combining age band, employer, and admission month. Which failure and remedy pair is correct?
options: Backups were not encrypted; encrypt them
The data was encrypted with too short a key; lengthen it
The survey used TLS 1.2; upgrade to TLS 1.3
Quasi-identifiers enabled a linkage attack; remedy by further generalization, suppression of risky combinations, and pre-release re-identification testing
explain: Re-identification happened through quasi-identifier linkage (B), so the fix is stronger de-identification and adversarial testing before release. The released data was not an encryption problem (A). Backup encryption (C) and TLS versions (D) protect other states and would not have changed what the published fields reveal.

q: A cloud provider runs customer VMs directly on hardware with no host operating system. Which hypervisor type is this, and why is it preferred?
options: Type 2 (hosted), because it isolates guests more strongly
Type 2 (hosted), because it removes the need for patching
Type 1 (bare-metal), with a smaller attack surface and better performance
Type 1 (bare-metal), because it allows nested virtualization by default
explain: Type 1 hypervisors run directly on hardware (A), preferred for production clouds for performance and a reduced attack surface. (B) is wrong because Type 2 runs atop a host OS with a larger attack surface and weaker isolation. (C) is wrong because nested virtualization is not the reason for the preference. (D) is wrong because Type 2 still requires patching the host OS.

q: An attacker compromises a guest VM and then exploits the hypervisor to access other tenants' VMs. What is this attack called, and why is it the MOST severe virtualization threat?
options: VM hopping via the virtual network
VM sprawl, because it wastes resources
VM escape, because it breaks the isolation boundary protecting all tenants
Snapshot revert, because it restores old vulnerabilities
explain: VM escape (C) breaks out of the guest to the hypervisor or host, compromising the isolation boundary every tenant relies on, which is why it is the most severe virtualization threat. Sprawl (A) is wrong because it is a management problem, not an attack. Network-based VM hopping (B) is wrong because segmentation can contain it; escape defeats the hypervisor itself. Snapshot revert (D) is wrong because it affects one VM's state, not the isolation boundary.

q: A company discovers 300 untracked VMs, many unpatched and running unauthorized services. What is the PRIMARY risk, and the BEST remediation?
options: Slow performance; add more hosts
Cost overruns; delete all VMs immediately
License violations; buy more licenses
Expanded attack surface; implement VM lifecycle management with automated provisioning and decommissioning
explain: Sprawl expands the attack surface with unmanaged, unpatched systems, and lifecycle management with automation (D) fixes the root cause. (A) is wrong because blind deletion could destroy production workloads. (B) addresses only licensing. (C) treats a symptom while the unmanaged systems remain.

q: A team debates containers versus VMs for a microservices platform. Which statement is TRUE?
options: Containers each include a full guest OS, making them heavier than VMs
Containers provide stronger isolation than Type 1 hypervisors
VMs cannot run microservices architectures
Containers share the host OS kernel using namespaces and cgroups, making them lighter but dependent on kernel isolation
explain: Containers share the host kernel via namespaces and cgroups (B), which makes them lightweight but dependent on kernel-level isolation. (A) reverses the facts. (C) is wrong because hypervisor isolation is stronger than container isolation. (D) is wrong because VMs run microservices fine, just with more overhead.

q: Before deploying containers, a bank verifies each image is signed by its build pipeline and scanned for CVEs. Which risks do these controls address?
options: Network eavesdropping between containers
Kernel privilege escalation only
Excessive container startup time
Image tampering and known vulnerabilities from untrusted provenance
explain: Signing proves provenance and integrity while scanning finds known CVEs in image layers (A). (B) is wrong because these controls do not fix kernel bugs. (C) is wrong because network encryption is a separate control. (D) is wrong because startup time is a performance matter.

q: In a serverless (FaaS) application, which responsibilities remain with the CUSTOMER?
options: Securing application code, IAM roles, and event-source inputs
Securing the physical data center
Patching the underlying host operating systems
Managing the function runtime environment
explain: In FaaS the provider manages hosts and runtimes, so the customer still owns code security, least-privilege function roles, and validating event inputs (D). (A), (B), and (C) are all provider responsibilities in the serverless model.

q: An architect wants to limit lateral movement so a compromised web tier cannot reach the database tier. Which control BEST achieves this?
options: Disabling all logging
A single perimeter firewall
Micro-segmentation with workload-level policies
VLAN trunking everywhere
explain: Micro-segmentation (C) enforces granular east-west policies between workloads, containing lateral movement. A perimeter firewall (A) is wrong because it only guards north-south traffic. VLAN trunking (B) is wrong because it extends broadcast domains rather than segmenting. (D) is wrong and nonsensical.

q: A cloud engineer needs a stateful filter applied at the instance level that automatically allows return traffic. Which should she use?
options: Security group, because it is stateful and instance-level
Network ACL, because it is stateful
Network ACL, because it applies at the instance
Route table, because it filters traffic
explain: Security groups (B) are stateful and attach to instances, so return traffic is automatically allowed. (A) is wrong because NACLs are stateless. (C) is wrong because NACLs apply at the subnet level. (D) is wrong because route tables direct traffic rather than filter it.

q: Administrators need SSH access to private-subnet servers with no public IPs. Which design BEST secures this management access?
options: A hardened bastion/jump host in a public subnet with MFA and session logging
Share one root password among admins
Assign public IPs to all servers temporarily
Open SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 on each server
explain: A bastion host (D) centralizes administrative access with hardening, MFA, and auditing. (A) exposes servers directly to the internet. (B) opens SSH to the entire internet. (C) violates accountability and least privilege.

q: A team standardizes hardened VM images using published secure-configuration benchmarks. Which sources are the industry standard for these baselines?
options: PCI DSS SAQs
NIST SP 800-61
CIS Benchmarks and DISA STIGs
OWASP Top 10
explain: CIS Benchmarks and DISA STIGs (A) are the industry-standard secure-configuration baselines for hardening. OWASP Top 10 (B) is wrong because it covers web application risks, not OS hardening. NIST SP 800-61 (C) is wrong because it is the incident response guide. PCI DSS SAQs (D) are wrong because they are compliance self-assessments.

q: A cloud team replaces entire VM images with freshly patched golden images rather than patching running servers. What is this approach called, and what is its main security benefit?
options: Manual patching; more control
Snapshot patching; smaller images
In-place patching; faster rollback
Immutable infrastructure; consistent, drift-free systems
explain: Immutable infrastructure (C) redeploys from known-good images, eliminating configuration drift. (A) is wrong because in-place patching is the opposite approach. (B) is wrong because manual patching increases drift and human error. (D) is not a standard term and misstates the benefit.

q: After an outage, the business can tolerate 4 hours of downtime but only 15 minutes of data loss. Which statement is TRUE?
options: RTO is 4 hours and RPO is 15 minutes
RTO and RPO are both 4 hours
RTO is 15 minutes and RPO is 4 hours
RPO measures downtime and RTO measures data loss
explain: RTO is the maximum tolerable downtime (4 hours) and RPO is the maximum tolerable data-loss window (15 minutes) (B). (A) swaps the two, a classic exam trap. (C) conflates them, and (D) reverses the definitions: RTO always measures time down, RPO always measures data at risk.

q: A company needs failover within minutes with near-zero data loss for a critical database. Which combination BEST meets this?
options: Pilot light with manual DNS change
Synchronous replication to a warm standby or multi-site active configuration
Weekly tape backup stored offsite
Cold site activated within 48 hours
explain: Synchronous replication with warm standby or multi-site active-active (D) gives minute-level failover with minimal data loss. (A) is wrong because weekly backups mean a large RPO and slow restore. (B) is wrong because pilot light requires scaling up, taking longer. (C) is wrong because cold sites take hours to days to activate.

q: A cloud provider wants assurance that a host booted only signed, untampered firmware and OS components. Which technology BEST provides this?
options: TPM-based measured/secure boot with remote attestation
Full-disk encryption alone
A bastion host
A software firewall
explain: TPM-based measured boot (B) cryptographically verifies each boot component and attests the result remotely. A firewall (A) is wrong because it filters network traffic, not boot integrity. Disk encryption alone (C) is wrong because it protects data at rest, not the boot chain. A bastion host (D) is wrong because it secures administrative access.

q: In a software-defined network, which statement BEST describes the architecture?
options: VLANs cannot be used with SDN
The data plane and control plane are fused in hardware
The control plane is separated from the data plane and centrally programmable
Each switch makes independent routing decisions with no central view
explain: SDN separates the control plane, run by a centralized controller, from the data plane of forwarding devices (D). (A) describes traditional distributed networking. (B) is the opposite of SDN. (C) is wrong because SDN commonly orchestrates VLANs and VXLAN overlays.

q: Which design BEST protects a cloud management plane?
options: Shared credentials for the whole operations team
Disabling all management logging to reduce noise
Isolated admin network/VLAN, MFA, dedicated admin accounts, and audited jump hosts
Management interfaces reachable from the internet for convenience
explain: Isolating management traffic with MFA, dedicated accounts, and audited access (A) is the standard for protecting the management plane. (B) exposes the highest-privilege interfaces to attackers. (C) destroys accountability. (D) blinds defenders to administrative activity.

q: A provider needs millions of isolated tenant networks over shared physical infrastructure, exceeding the 4,094 VLAN limit. Which technology BEST solves this?
options: Hubs
Disabling segmentation
A single flat VLAN
VXLAN overlay networks
explain: VXLAN overlays (C) provide around 16 million segments over existing IP infrastructure, far beyond the VLAN limit. Hubs (A) are obsolete and provide no segmentation. A flat VLAN (B) is wrong because it provides no tenant isolation. (D) is wrong because it removes isolation entirely.

q: Developers run test VMs on their laptops using virtualization software installed on top of their desktop operating system. Which hypervisor type is this, and what is its main security drawback?
options: Type 2 hypervisor, because it runs on a host OS
Unikernel, because it is minimal
Type 1 hypervisor, because it is more secure
Container runtime, because it is lightweight
explain: A Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor (A) runs on top of a host operating system, so the host OS is an additional layer that must be patched and defended — the larger attack surface in the scenario. A Type 1 hypervisor (B) runs directly on hardware with no host OS. Container runtimes (C) share the host kernel rather than virtualizing hardware. Unikernels (D) are minimal single-purpose images, not hypervisors.

q: A tenant on shared cloud hardware notices another tenant's workload can infer its cryptographic keys by measuring cache access timing on the same physical CPU. What is this attack?
options: VM escape
Side-channel attack
Blue pill attack
Hyperjacking
explain: A side-channel attack (C) extracts secrets by observing shared physical resources — cache timing, power, or memory access patterns — without breaking VM isolation logically, matching the scenario. VM escape (A) breaks out of the guest to the hypervisor. Hyperjacking (B) installs a rogue hypervisor beneath the OS. Blue pill (D) is a specific hypervisor-based rootkit technique.

q: An attacker compromises one container in a Kubernetes pod and exploits a host kernel vulnerability to gain access to the underlying node and neighboring containers. What is this called?
options: VM escape
Container escape
Rootkit installation
Hypervisor escape
explain: Container escape (B) exploits the shared host kernel that all containers on a node use — a kernel vulnerability lets an attacker break out of the container to the host. VM escape (A) targets a hypervisor, not a shared kernel. Hypervisor escape (C) is the same as VM escape. A rootkit (D) is a persistence technique, not the breakout itself.

q: A platform team wants Kubernetes to automatically reject any pod whose container image is not signed by the corporate build pipeline. Which control enforces this at deploy time?
options: A service mesh
Admission controllers
etcd encryption
The kubelet agent
explain: Admission controllers (D) intercept API requests before objects are persisted and can enforce policies such as 'only images from the approved registry with a valid signature.' The kubelet (A) runs pods but does not set policy. etcd encryption (B) protects stored cluster state. A service mesh (C) manages service-to-service traffic, not deployment admission.

q: A web server in a private subnet can initiate outbound HTTPS connections, but the responses never arrive. The security group allows all outbound traffic and the subnet uses a custom NACL. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The NACL is blocking all traffic by default
NACLs are stateless, so return traffic needs an explicit inbound rule
The route table is misconfigured
Security groups are stateful, so return traffic is automatic
explain: NACLs are stateless (A): unlike stateful security groups, they do not automatically allow return traffic, so the ephemeral-port range must be explicitly permitted inbound for responses to return. Security groups being stateful (B) is true but does not fix the NACL. NACLs do not block all traffic by default (C) — default NACLs allow all. A route table issue (D) would break outbound initiation too, but outbound works here.

q: An attacker exploits a server-side request forgery flaw in a web app to query the cloud instance metadata service and steal the attached IAM role credentials. Which control BEST mitigates this attack class?
options: Enforce IMDSv2 and restrict instance metadata access
Disable TLS on the application
Move to a larger instance type
Open the security group to the internet
explain: The attack abused the instance metadata service, so the fix is enforcing IMDSv2 (session-oriented, harder to exploit via SSRF) and restricting metadata access (C). Disabling TLS (A) worsens security. Opening the security group (B) expands exposure. A larger instance (D) is irrelevant to SSRF.

q: A cloud-hosted storefront faces a 500 Gbps volumetric DDoS attack during a product launch. Which design BEST keeps the site available?
options: Block all ICMP at the border
A single stateful firewall
Null-routing the target IPs
Edge-based scrubbing with elastic scaling behind it
explain: Volumetric DDoS is best absorbed at the provider edge with scrubbing/CDN capacity plus elastic scaling (B) so legitimate traffic survives. Blocking ICMP (A) does not stop large UDP/TCP floods. A single firewall (C) becomes the bottleneck and fails first. Null-routing (D) takes the victim offline — the attacker's goal.

q: A non-critical reporting system can tolerate 48 hours of downtime, and the business wants the cheapest recovery option. Which DR site type fits?
options: Warm site
Cold site
Hot site
Active-active multi-site
explain: A cold site (D) is the cheapest option — reserved space with no provisioned infrastructure — appropriate when the business accepts a long recovery window for non-critical systems. Hot (A), warm (B), and active-active (C) sites all cost significantly more for faster recovery the business does not require here.

q: A company replicates its database continuously to a second region but keeps application servers as machine images that are launched only during failover. Which DR approach is this?
options: Cold site
Backup and restore
Pilot light
Hot standby
explain: Pilot light (A) keeps a minimal core — typically the replicated database — running in the recovery region, with remaining servers provisioned from images at failover time: faster than backup-and-restore, cheaper than hot standby. Hot standby (B) runs full capacity continuously. Cold site (C) has nothing provisioned. Backup and restore (D) is the slowest approach.

q: A SaaS application runs actively in two regions. During a regional outage, users must be routed to the healthy region within minutes with no manual intervention. Which design achieves this?
options: Require a manual DNS change ticket during outages
Keep a single region and hope for the best
Notify customers by email instead of failing over
DNS-based failover with automated health checks
explain: DNS-based failover with health checks (C) automatically reroutes users to the healthy region when checks fail — the standard multi-region web pattern. A single region (A) has no failover. Manual ticket-driven changes (B) are too slow. Email notification (D) is communication, not recovery.

q: A team uses immutable golden images, but engineers keep 'temporarily' tweaking running servers, and the fleet slowly diverges from the approved baseline. Which control BEST addresses this?
options: Disable all logging to save cost
Ignore drift; it resolves itself
Annual manual audits
Continuous configuration drift detection against the baseline
explain: Continuous drift detection (B) compares running configurations against the approved baseline and flags unauthorized changes for remediation — the control that keeps immutable infrastructure honest. Ignoring drift (A) lets snowflake servers reappear. Annual audits (C) leave an 11-month blind spot. Disabling logging (D) destroys the evidence needed for detection.

q: A cloud team wants assurance that a VM booted only untampered firmware and OS components, and that its disk-encryption keys cannot be used if the boot chain was modified. Which technology provides both?
options: A shared HSM partition
A software keystore on the VM
Plaintext keys in instance metadata
A virtual TPM for measured boot and key sealing
explain: A virtual TPM (D) provides hardware-rooted measured boot — verifying each boot component — and seals disk-encryption keys so they only unseal on an untampered boot. A software keystore (A) lacks hardware protection. A shared HSM partition (B) does not attest to the VM's boot integrity. Plaintext keys in metadata (C) are trivially stealable.

q: An application in a private subnet must reach a managed cloud database service without any traffic crossing the public internet. Which design achieves this?
options: A public IP on every database
Private connectivity via VPC endpoints or PrivateLink
Database credentials in application code
Port-forwarding through a developer laptop
explain: VPC endpoints/PrivateLink (A) expose cloud services to the VPC over private network paths with no internet traversal — the secure pattern. Public IPs on databases (B) invite direct attack. Credentials in code (C) leak secrets. Port-forwarding through a laptop (D) is fragile and unauditable.

q: A cloud web application is protected by both a WAF and instance security groups. Which statement BEST describes how these controls relate?
options: A WAF makes security groups unnecessary
Security groups can inspect SQL injection payloads
They are complementary layers: the WAF inspects HTTP payloads while security groups filter network traffic
A WAF encrypts traffic between tiers
explain: They are complementary layers (B): the WAF operates at Layer 7, inspecting HTTP payloads for injection and XSS, while security groups filter at Layers 3/4 by IP, port, and protocol. A WAF does not replace network filtering (A). Security groups cannot parse application payloads (C). A WAF does not encrypt traffic (D) — TLS does.

q: Administrators use a bastion host to reach production servers. Auditors require proof of exactly which commands each administrator ran during privileged sessions. Which control BEST provides this?
options: Require MFA and record privileged sessions on the bastion
Allow direct SSH from the internet with key auth
Share one admin password among the team
Disable all logging to reduce storage cost
explain: MFA plus session recording (C) gives strong authentication for privileged access and an audit trail of exactly what each administrator did — the accountability requirement. Shared passwords (A) destroy attribution. Internet-exposed SSH (B) invites brute force. Disabling logging (D) eliminates the evidence needed for accountability.

q: An architect needs deep packet inspection with TLS decryption between application tiers inside a cloud VPC, to catch malware in east-west traffic. Which control provides this?
options: The host operating system firewall alone
A virtual next-generation firewall appliance
A NACL alone
A security group alone
explain: A virtual NGFW appliance (A) provides Layer 7 inspection — including TLS decryption and intrusion prevention — inside the VPC, which neither security groups nor NACLs can do. Security groups (B) and NACLs (C) only filter by IP/port/protocol. A host firewall (D) protects one machine, not inter-tier traffic.

q: A payment service must stay online even if an entire cloud region fails. Which architecture meets this requirement?
options: Rely on multi-AZ within one region
Active-active deployment across multiple regions
Deploy in a single availability zone
Keep backups in the same region
explain: Only active-active multi-region (D) survives a full regional outage with no downtime — multi-AZ (B) protects against zone failure but shares the region's fate. A single AZ (A) is the weakest posture. Same-region backups (C) aid recovery but do not keep the service running during the outage.

q: During a hypervisor configuration review, an assessor finds the hypervisor management interface reachable from the same virtual switch that carries untrusted tenant workloads. What is the BEST remediation?
options: Leave the interface in place but rename the management virtual switch
Disable hypervisor logging so attackers cannot discover the interface
Move hypervisor management onto a physically or logically separate management network reachable only from an admin segment
Publish the management interface through the tenant load balancer for redundancy
explain: Management traffic must be segregated onto its own isolated network (C) so a tenant-side compromise cannot reach the controls that own every guest. Renaming a switch (A) is cosmetic and changes no reachability. Exposing management through a tenant load balancer (B) widens the attack surface. Disabling logging (D) removes detection without removing exposure.

q: A development lead proposes hosting a production card-processing workload on laptops running a hosted hypervisor installed over a general-purpose desktop OS, arguing it saves licensing costs. What is the PRIMARY security objection?
options: Guests on a hosted hypervisor cannot be patched
A compromise of the underlying desktop OS and its applications can undermine every guest running above it
Hosted hypervisors cannot encrypt virtual disks
Desktop hardware cannot use virtual networking
explain: A Type 2 hosted hypervisor inherits the host OS attack surface (B): malware or a flaw in the desktop OS, browser, or office apps can reach the hypervisor and its guests, which is unacceptable for production payment workloads. Hosted products can encrypt disks (A) and guests can be patched (C). Virtual networking is supported (D); none of those are the core objection.

q: A hypervisor vendor discloses a flaw in an emulated virtual device that lets a guest execute code in the hypervisor context. The provider cannot patch every host instantly. Which action MOST reduces risk during the patch window?
options: Disable or remove the vulnerable virtual device from guest configurations and live-migrate guests to already-patched hosts
Enable nested virtualization so guests can inspect the hypervisor
Take guest snapshots so tenants can roll back after an escape
Increase guest memory reservations until patching completes
explain: Removing the vulnerable device closes the specific escape path and migrating to patched hosts eliminates it (D). Memory reservations (A) affect performance, not the flaw. Snapshots (B) preserve state but do not stop hypervisor compromise. Nested virtualization (C) expands privileged surface and helps an attacker, not the defender.

q: After a reorganization, a security engineer finds a powered-off virtual machine that has been dormant for nine months being switched back on and reconnected straight to the production segment. What should happen FIRST?
options: Let it connect, because a powered-off machine cannot have changed
Delete the machine immediately without inspection
Clone it so a spare copy exists before anyone logs in
Place it in a quarantine segment, scan and patch it, and verify its purpose and owner before production access
explain: A dormant VM misses months of patches and may hold stale credentials or unauthorized software, so it must be quarantined, assessed, and re-authorized before production access (A). Powering off freezes its patch state rather than making it safe (B). Immediate deletion (C) may destroy a needed asset or evidence. Cloning (D) replicates the risk.

q: A golden template review shows virtual floppy drives, CD-ROM devices, clipboard sharing, and drag-and-drop enabled on every server built from it, none of which operations uses. What is the BEST hardening action?
options: Remove or disable the unused virtual devices and guest-host integration features in the template
Enable every virtual device so future teams have flexibility
Move the template to an unencrypted datastore for faster builds
Share the template credentials with all administrators
explain: Unused virtual devices and integration features are pure attack surface, so disabling them in the template hardens every clone built from it (B). Enabling more features (A) does the opposite. An unencrypted datastore (C) endangers the template itself. Sharing template credentials (D) destroys accountability and widens access.

q: Forensics on a cloned server fleet shows every clone shares the same local administrator password, the same SSH host keys, and the same machine identity because templates were copied without generalization. What is the root failure and BEST fix?
options: The hypervisor was Type 1; move clones to a hosted hypervisor
Clones were given too much RAM; reduce memory allocations
Disk encryption was missing; enable full-disk encryption on clones
Templates were not generalized before cloning; sysprep/generalize templates and inject unique credentials and host keys per clone at build time
explain: Copying an ungeneralized image duplicates identities and secrets across the fleet, so one credential compromise becomes a fleet compromise; generalization plus per-clone unique secrets fixes the root cause (B). Disk encryption (A) protects data at rest but not shared credentials. Hypervisor type (C) is irrelevant to image hygiene. Memory sizing (D) is a performance setting.

q: A storage administrator warns leadership that virtual machine snapshots are being treated as a free backup system. Which TWO risks of long-lived snapshots should the security team emphasize? (Choose two.)
options: Snapshots reduce the size of the underlying virtual disk over time
Reverting to an old snapshot can silently reintroduce patched vulnerabilities and revoked credentials
Snapshots stored with the VM can expose full disk and memory contents, including secrets, if the datastore is accessed
Snapshots automatically encrypt themselves with tenant-managed keys
explain: Long-lived snapshots are complete copies of disk (and sometimes memory) that inherit none of the care given to backups, so datastore access exposes their secrets (A), and a revert rolls the guest back to an old patch and credential state (C). Snapshots are not automatically encrypted with tenant keys (B). They grow storage consumption and degrade performance rather than shrinking disks (D).

q: Operations keeps production snapshots for six months 'just in case,' and performance and datastore incidents are rising. Which policy BEST balances recoverability and risk?
options: Keep snapshots indefinitely but hide them from the inventory
Disable snapshot capability on all virtual machines permanently
Convert every snapshot into a permanent template
Use snapshots only as short-term pre-change protection with a defined maximum lifetime, and use a real backup system for retention
explain: Snapshots are a short-term change-protection tool, not a retention mechanism; capping their lifetime and using purpose-built backups for retention addresses both performance and exposure (D). Hiding snapshots (A) removes oversight. Templates (B) multiply unmanaged copies. Disabling snapshots entirely (C) removes a legitimate operational control instead of governing it.

q: An audit of the virtualization estate finds shared local hypervisor accounts, no multi-factor authentication on the virtualization console, and hypervisor logs retained only on each host. Which remediation set BEST addresses the findings?
options: Unique named admin accounts with MFA, and hypervisor logs forwarded to a central tamper-resistant log platform
Logs deleted daily so they cannot be tampered with
Console access restricted to business hours only
A longer shared password rotated once a year
explain: Hypervisor consoles control every guest, so they need attributable unique accounts, MFA, and off-host centralized logging that survives a host compromise (D). A shared password, however long (A), still destroys attribution. Time-of-day limits (B) do not fix identity or logging. Deleting logs (C) eliminates the audit trail auditors require.

q: Two workload zones of very different sensitivity share one host cluster. A misconfigured trunk on a shared virtual switch briefly placed a low-trust test VM on the restricted production port group. What is the BEST architectural response for the highest-sensitivity workloads?
options: Encrypt guest disks and leave the network design unchanged
Place the highest-sensitivity workloads on a dedicated cluster with separate virtual switching and verified port-group change control
Give the test VM a static IP address on the restricted network
Accept the risk because trunk errors are rare
explain: For the highest assurance, physical or cluster-level separation removes dependence on a single tagging configuration being perfect, backed by change control on port groups (C). Accepting the risk (A) ignores a demonstrated failure. A static IP (B) does not fix layer-2 placement. Disk encryption (D) protects storage, not network segmentation.

q: A private-cloud operator must prove that one department's runaway workload cannot starve or observe the workloads of other departments on shared hosts. Which TWO hypervisor-level controls MOST directly support this? (Choose two.)
options: Placing all departments in a single resource pool with no boundaries
A shared local administrator account for all departments
Enforced guest isolation settings that disable inter-VM data paths such as shared clipboard and device sharing
Resource shares, limits, and reservations that cap each tenant's CPU and memory consumption
explain: Resource controls bound consumption so a noisy neighbor cannot starve others (A), and disabling guest-to-guest convenience channels removes unintended data paths between tenants (D). A shared admin account (B) weakens attribution and isolation. A single unbounded resource pool (C) is exactly the condition the operator must disprove.

q: A migration review notes that live-migration traffic between hosts crosses the general production network in cleartext, carrying full guest memory contents. What is the BEST control?
options: Send migration traffic through the tenant-facing load balancer
Compress migration traffic so its contents are harder to read
Disable live migration and power off guests for every move
Run live migration over a dedicated isolated network and enable encrypted migration where the platform supports it
explain: Guest memory contains keys and credentials, so migration needs an isolated network and encryption in transit (B). Compression (A) is not confidentiality. Disabling migration (C) sacrifices availability and patching agility unnecessarily. Routing memory contents through a tenant load balancer (D) exposes them further.

q: A regulated tenant's contract states its workloads must never run on the same physical host as workloads belonging to other companies, and auditors will test the claim. Which deployment BEST satisfies this?
options: Dedicated hosts or a dedicated cluster assigned exclusively to that tenant, with placement rules preventing co-residency
A shared cluster with anti-affinity rules between the tenant's own VMs
Larger VM sizes so the tenant dominates any host it lands on
Standard multi-tenant hosts with strong security groups
explain: Only dedicated hosts or clusters give an auditable guarantee of no co-residency (A). Security groups (B) control network traffic, not physical placement. Anti-affinity between the tenant's own VMs (C) spreads its VMs but says nothing about other tenants. VM size (D) never guarantees exclusive occupancy.

q: A host-by-host hypervisor patch cycle keeps stalling because no host can be emptied during business hours. Which approach lets patching proceed WITHOUT downtime for tenants?
options: Skip hypervisor patches that require host reboots
Snapshot every guest and accept a full-cluster outage
Patch hosts in place while guests keep running
Live-migrate guests off each host in turn, patch and reboot the empty host, then rebalance
explain: Rolling maintenance using live migration empties one host at a time so it can be patched and rebooted while service continues elsewhere (D). In-place patching of a running hypervisor (A) is generally not possible for kernel-level fixes. Skipping reboot-required patches (B) leaves known escape paths open. A full outage (C) is what the approach exists to avoid.

q: A cluster's image registry allows anonymous pulls, and several production images are publicly readable. What is the FIRST corrective action?
options: Delete all images and rebuild the cluster
Move the registry to a faster storage tier
Make the registry private, require authenticated pulls, and scope repository access by team
Rename the images so they are harder to guess
explain: Registry exposure is an access-control failure: requiring authentication and per-repository authorization stops unauthenticated disclosure and substitution of production images (C). Obscure names (A) are not a control. Storage tiering (B) is irrelevant. Deleting everything (D) is destructive and unnecessary.

q: A node-hardening review finds kubelet anonymous authentication enabled, an unauthenticated read-only kubelet port open, and unrestricted SSH from the office network to every worker node. Which finding is MOST dangerous and why?
options: SSH access, because SSH is an insecure protocol
The read-only kubelet port, because it can disclose pod and environment details including secrets to anyone who can reach it
None of them, because worker nodes hold no sensitive data
Anonymous authentication, because it slows API responses
explain: An unauthenticated kubelet endpoint can enumerate pods and return environment variables and mounted secret data from that node to any network-adjacent attacker, making it the most immediately exploitable finding (C). SSH itself is encrypted and standard when controlled (A). Anonymous auth is serious but (B) misstates its impact as performance. Worker nodes run the workloads and their secrets, so (D) is false.

q: A platform team exposes the Kubernetes API server to the internet so remote developers can use kubectl from home. Which design change BEST preserves access while protecting the control plane?
options: Keep the public endpoint and rely on strong passwords
Restrict the API server to known source ranges or private access, front it with SSO/OIDC and MFA, and enable API audit logging
Disable RBAC so developers stop hitting permission errors
Move the API server behind the application ingress used by customers
explain: Control-plane protection means minimizing who can reach the API and strongly authenticating and auditing those who can (C). Passwords alone (A) invite credential stuffing against a cluster-admin endpoint. Disabling RBAC (B) grants everyone cluster power. Sharing the customer ingress (D) mixes the highest-privilege plane with public application traffic.

q: A cluster currently permits every pod to talk to every other pod across all namespaces. The platform team must introduce network segmentation. Which TWO steps are MOST effective? (Choose two.)
options: Give every pod a host network address so traffic is easier to trace
Apply a default-deny NetworkPolicy for ingress and egress in each namespace, then add explicit allow policies per application flow
Rely on namespace names alone to keep workloads apart
Select a CNI that actually enforces NetworkPolicy, since policies are inert if the plugin ignores them
explain: Default-deny plus explicit allows turns the flat network into least-privilege segmentation (C), but it only works if the CNI enforces policies, which not all plugins do (D). Namespaces alone provide no traffic isolation (A). Host networking (B) removes pod network isolation and increases exposure.

q: A developer argues that Kubernetes Secrets are safe to commit to the manifest repository because they are 'encrypted.' What is the CORRECT response and remedy?
options: Base64 is only encoding, so anyone with the repo or etcd can read the values; use an external secrets manager or sealed/encrypted secrets with etcd encryption at rest
She is right; base64 is an encryption standard
Print secrets into container logs so they are backed up
Secrets are safe as long as the repository is large
explain: Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted, by default (C); real protection needs etcd encryption at rest, tight RBAC on secret reads, or an external vault that injects values at runtime. (A) repeats the misconception being corrected. Repository size (B) is irrelevant. Logging secrets (D) spreads them into another system.

q: A workload requests a privileged container with host PID and network namespaces and a hostPath mount of the node root filesystem 'for troubleshooting.' What is the security verdict?
options: Approve it only on Fridays when staffing is higher
Approve it if the image passed a vulnerability scan
Approve it; privileged mode is required for logging agents
Deny it as designed; that combination is effectively root on the node and a container-escape path, so use a scoped debug approach instead
explain: Privileged mode plus host namespaces and a root hostPath mount removes the container boundary, giving node-level root and access to every co-located pod (A). Image scanning (D) cannot make a deliberately boundary-less configuration safe. Troubleshooting has narrower tools (ephemeral debug containers, node-shell with approval) so (B) and scheduling tricks (C) are unjustified.

q: A deployment pipeline references images by the mutable 'latest' tag, and an incident shows production pulled a different image than the one tested, with no malicious act involved. Which practice prevents recurrence?
options: Rebuild the image more frequently
Pin deployments to immutable image digests and prohibit mutable tags in production namespaces
Rename 'latest' to 'newest' so intent is clearer
Increase the number of replicas so a bad image is diluted
explain: Digest pinning makes the tested artifact and the deployed artifact cryptographically identical and prevents silent substitution (B). Rebuild frequency (A) increases variance. Renaming a mutable tag (C) changes nothing. More replicas (D) spread, rather than prevent, a wrong image.

q: A security review discovers the cluster's etcd datastore is unencrypted, its client port is reachable from the general corporate network, and etcd backups sit in a broadly readable bucket. Which statement BEST captures the risk?
options: Risk is limited to performance degradation of the API server
Critical risk, because etcd holds the full cluster state including Secrets, and both live access and backups must be restricted and encrypted
Low risk, because etcd stores only scheduling metadata
The only issue is backup retention length
explain: Etcd is the cluster's source of truth and stores Secrets in readable form unless encrypted, so network exposure and readable backups are a direct path to every credential in the cluster (D). (A) understates etcd's contents. Retention (B) is secondary to confidentiality. (C) ignores the data exposure entirely.

q: Image scans are clean, yet a deployed container begins beaconing and mining cryptocurrency two days after release. Which capability would MOST likely have detected this?
options: Longer image retention in the registry
Runtime security monitoring that profiles container behavior and alerts on deviations such as unexpected processes and outbound connections
Checking the image size against last week's build
A second static image scanner from a different vendor
explain: The compromise happened at runtime, so behavioral runtime monitoring that sees new processes, shells, and egress is the control that detects it (A). Another static scanner (B) inspects the same clean image. Retention (C) and image size (D) are not detection mechanisms for post-deploy compromise.

q: Every pod in a namespace automatically receives a mounted service account token, but most of the applications never call the Kubernetes API. What is the BEST hardening step?
options: Disable automatic token mounting for workloads that do not need API access, and give each application its own minimally-scoped service account
Base64-encode the tokens before mounting them
Grant the default service account cluster-admin so token use never fails
Rotate the cluster CA weekly
explain: Unneeded API tokens are stolen-credential material in every compromised pod; disabling automount and using per-app least-privilege accounts removes that exposure (B). CA rotation (A) does not change token scope. Cluster-admin (C) maximizes the damage of token theft. Tokens are already encoded in transit to pods, so (D) adds nothing.

q: A bank runs a shared cluster where an untrusted analytics team's batch jobs share worker nodes with payment pods, separated only by namespaces. A kernel exploit in a batch job could reach payment data. Which architecture BEST matches the bank's isolation need?
options: Increase CPU limits on the payment pods
Keep shared nodes and add more namespace labels
Move regulated workloads to dedicated node pools or a separate cluster, using taints and tolerations to keep untrusted jobs off those nodes
Rely on container image scanning to prevent kernel exploits
explain: Namespaces are an administrative boundary, not a kernel isolation boundary; co-locating hostile and regulated workloads on one kernel is the flaw, and dedicated nodes or clusters restore a real boundary (A). Labels (B) enforce nothing. CPU limits (C) address resources, not escape. Scanning (D) cannot guarantee a kernel has no exploitable flaw.

q: An orchestration security baseline is being written for a new production cluster. Which TWO control-plane protections belong in the baseline? (Choose two.)
options: Store cluster-admin kubeconfig files on a shared team drive for convenience
Allow unauthenticated health endpoints from any network
Encrypt etcd at rest using a KMS-backed encryption configuration
Enable Kubernetes audit logging and forward API audit events to the SIEM
explain: Audit logging shipped off-cluster gives visibility into who did what through the API (C), and KMS-backed etcd encryption protects stored Secrets and state (D). Shared cluster-admin kubeconfigs (A) hand out unrestricted, unattributable power. Unauthenticated endpoints from anywhere (B) invite probing of the control plane.

q: Production registries accept image pushes from any engineer's workstation, and a review cannot prove a running image came from the reviewed pipeline. What is the BEST registry control?
options: Allow pushes but require a comment describing the change
Delete workstation Docker installations
Restrict push rights to the build pipeline's identity only, and require deployment admission checks that the image digest was produced by that pipeline
Make all production images public so anyone can verify them
explain: Limiting who can publish to the pipeline identity and verifying provenance at admission closes both the direct-push bypass and the proof gap (C). Comments (A) are unverifiable. Public images (B) disclose proprietary code and still prove nothing about origin. Engineers legitimately need local tooling (D); the defect is registry trust, not Docker's existence.

q: A multi-team cluster lets each team create pods with no restrictions, and one team routinely runs host-network, privileged debug pods in its namespace. Which platform control BEST constrains this without reviewing every manifest by hand?
options: A ticket queue for manual manifest approval
Pod Security Standards admission set to enforce the restricted profile on tenant namespaces, with narrowly scoped exemptions
A wiki page asking teams not to run privileged pods
Nightly reports listing privileged pods for discussion
explain: Built-in Pod Security admission enforces the restricted profile automatically at deploy time, blocking privileged and host-network pods before they run (B). Manual queues (A) do not scale and are bypass-prone. A wiki (C) is advisory. Nightly reports (D) detect after exposure rather than preventing it.

q: A design diagram shows database instances in a subnet whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway, each with a public address 'for vendor support.' What is the BEST correction?
options: Move databases to private subnets with no internet-gateway route and reach them only through the application tier or approved private connectivity
Publish the database addresses in DNS so the vendor can find them
Keep the design but choose complex database passwords
Add a second internet gateway for redundancy
explain: Databases should have no public path at all; private subnets without an internet route remove the entire class of direct internet attack and misconfiguration risk (D). Password strength (A) does not justify public exposure. More gateways (B) or DNS publication (C) increase reachability.

q: A VPC hosts a three-tier application across two availability zones. Which layout BEST follows segmentation practice?
options: All tiers in public subnets, relying on host firewalls
A single private subnet for everything, including the load balancer
Separate subnets per tier per zone: public subnets only for load balancers, private subnets for application and data tiers
One large subnet spanning all tiers and zones
explain: Per-tier, per-zone subnets let routing and filtering differ by trust level and survive a zone failure (B). One flat subnet (A) defeats segmentation. Public placement of all tiers (C) exposes layers that never need it. Putting the internet-facing load balancer in a private subnet (D) breaks the design.

q: A security team must explicitly BLOCK traffic from a known malicious address range; every other control they use only permits traffic. Which cloud network control supports an explicit deny?
options: Route tables, because they can blackhole by omission
Security groups, because they evaluate deny rules first
Network ACLs, because they support numbered allow and deny rules evaluated in order
Security groups, because returning traffic is denied by default
explain: Network ACLs support explicit deny rules (A), while security groups are allow-only, so blocking a hostile range at the subnet boundary requires the ACL. (B) invents deny evaluation in security groups. Route tables (C) direct traffic but are not a filtering policy mechanism for this purpose. (D) misstates security group behavior, which is stateful.

q: After an ACL change, legitimate application traffic to a subnet stops even though a broad allow rule exists further down the list. Investigation finds a lower-numbered deny rule matching the traffic. What principle explains the outage?
options: Security groups overrode the ACL
Rule numbers are purely cosmetic labels
ACLs always prefer allow rules over deny rules
ACL rules are evaluated in ascending rule-number order and processing stops at the first match
explain: Stateless ACLs process rules from the lowest number upward and stop at the first match (D), so an early deny silently shadows later allows. (A) reverses how ordered evaluation works. Security groups (B) operate at a different layer and do not reorder ACL rules. (C) is false because numbering is the evaluation order.

q: A public web application is being placed behind a web application firewall. Which TWO placements give effective WAF coverage for its traffic paths? (Choose two.)
options: On a workstation in the developer's home
At the content delivery network edge, inspecting requests before they are forwarded to the origin
Inside the database server's storage volume
At the application load balancer that terminates traffic to the web tier
explain: A WAF must sit inline where HTTP traffic flows: at the CDN edge for internet requests (A) and/or at the load balancer fronting the web tier (B). A home workstation (C) is not in the traffic path. A storage volume (D) sees no HTTP requests to inspect.

q: An architect must inspect traffic between VPCs and the corporate data center, and also between two VPCs, through one managed inspection point rather than per-instance agents. Which design fits?
options: Placing a WAF in front of the database tier
Giving every instance a public address so traffic uses the internet
Disabling routing between VPCs entirely
A central security/transit VPC containing virtual firewall appliances through which inter-VPC and hybrid traffic is routed
explain: Routing traffic through a centralized inspection VPC with virtual firewalls gives one enforced checkpoint for north-south and east-west flows (B). Cutting all routing (A) breaks the business requirement. Public addressing (C) removes traffic from controlled paths. A WAF (D) inspects HTTP to web apps, not general inter-VPC network traffic.

q: A media site survives huge volumetric floods behind its scrubbing service, but a new attack of seemingly legitimate HTTP requests at moderate volume exhausts application workers. Which control MOST directly addresses this layer 7 flood?
options: Enabling flow logs on the VPC
Moving the database to a private subnet
WAF rate-based rules and bot controls at the CDN or load balancer, coupled with caching to absorb repeatable requests
A larger volumetric scrubbing contract
explain: Application-layer floods use valid requests, so they pass volumetric defenses; rate limiting, bot management, and caching at the edge or WAF shed them before they consume workers (D). More volumetric capacity (A) targets the wrong layer. Private subnets (B) and flow logs (C) are good practice but do not stop request floods.

q: Attackers bypass a site's CDN and WAF by sending requests straight to the origin load balancer's public address, which they found in old DNS records. What is the BEST fix?
options: Turn off the WAF so bypass attempts are less visible
Change the origin's DNS name weekly
Restrict the origin to accept only traffic from the CDN, using CDN address ranges, a secret validation header, or mutual TLS, and remove direct public exposure where possible
Ask the attackers' providers to block the traffic
explain: If the origin answers arbitrary internet clients, edge controls are optional for attackers; locking the origin to CDN-sourced, authenticated traffic restores the intended path (B). Provider complaints (A) are not an architecture. Rotating names (C) is obscurity that scanners defeat. Disabling the WAF (D) removes protection rather than fixing the bypass.

q: During incident response, investigators cannot tell which instance communicated with a command-and-control address last week because no network telemetry was retained. Which control should have been enabled?
options: Per-instance packet capture left running permanently
Longer DHCP leases
VPC flow logs delivered to centralized, retained log storage
A public IP inventory spreadsheet
explain: Flow logs record source, destination, ports, and disposition for VPC traffic and, when centralized and retained, answer exactly this forensic question (B). Permanent packet capture everywhere (A) is impractical and disproportionate. An IP spreadsheet (C) shows assignments, not communications. DHCP lease length (D) is unrelated to telemetry.

q: Application instances scale in and out constantly, and the database security group lists individual application IP addresses that go stale within hours. What is the BEST replacement?
options: Hard-code the addresses of future instances in advance
Disable the database security group and rely on passwords
Reference the application tier's security group as the allowed source in the database security group rule
Widen the database rule to the whole VPC range permanently
explain: Security-group referencing ties permission to workload identity rather than transient addresses, so it tracks autoscaling automatically (C). A whole-VPC range (A) grants every workload database access. Pre-guessing addresses (B) is unworkable. Removing the security group (D) deletes network authorization entirely.

q: A cloud architect must design outbound internet access for hundreds of private instances that need patching and API calls but must never accept inbound internet connections. Which TWO elements satisfy this? (Choose two.)
options: Route and security controls that permit egress only, combined with monitoring of outbound flows
A public IP address on every private instance
An internet gateway route added directly to each private subnet
A NAT gateway in a public subnet that translates outbound connections and returns their replies, while allowing no unsolicited inbound traffic
explain: A NAT gateway provides outbound-only connectivity with replies, without inbound reachability (A), and explicit egress-only rules with monitoring keep that posture governed (B). Public IPs on every instance (C) and direct internet-gateway routes (D) make the instances publicly addressable, violating the requirement.

q: One oversized shared VPC hosts development, production, and a newly acquired company's workloads, and a single misapplied route recently let development systems reach production databases. Which strategy BEST reduces this blast radius?
options: Add more subnets inside the same VPC
Give production databases stronger passwords
Rename the subnets to reflect their sensitivity
Separate environments into distinct VPCs or accounts with deliberately controlled interconnects, rather than one shared routing domain
explain: A single routing domain makes every routing mistake global; partitioning into separate VPCs or accounts with explicit, reviewed interconnects contains misconfigurations (B). Naming (A) changes nothing technical. More subnets in the same domain (C) keep shared fate. Passwords (D) do not address network reachability.

q: A transit gateway connects production, development, and shared-services VPCs. After a route change, development VPC traffic begins reaching production subnets that policy says must be unreachable from development. What is the MOST likely design flaw?
options: The transit gateway encrypts traffic between VPCs
The VPCs use overlapping address ranges
Development instances have flow logs enabled
Route tables and propagation were not segmented per environment, so routes leaked across trust boundaries
explain: Transit gateways isolate environments only if route tables and propagations are deliberately separated per trust zone; shared propagation leaks routes exactly as described (A). Encryption (B) is not the flaw. Overlap (C) would break routing rather than leak it selectively. Flow logs (D) only record traffic.

q: A post-breach review finds cloud workloads could initiate connections to any internet address on any port, which the attacker used for data staging and command-and-control. Which egress design BEST prevents recurrence?
options: Require MFA for instance logins
Allow all egress but log it after the fact
Default-deny egress from workload subnets, permitting only approved destinations through a controlled proxy or egress firewall with domain and port allowlists
Block inbound traffic more aggressively
explain: Default-deny egress with an allowlist through an inspected egress point removes arbitrary exfiltration and C2 channels (C). Logging unrestricted egress (A) observes rather than prevents. Inbound hardening (B) does not govern outbound staging. Login MFA (D) protects access, not workload egress.

q: A dual-stack VPC passes its IPv4 firewall review, but a scanner finds several instances reachable from the internet over IPv6 addresses that no rule was written for. What is the root cause and fix?
options: The scanner is wrong because IPv6 addresses are private by default
IPv6 cannot be filtered, so the VPC must be deleted
IPv6 traffic bypassed review because firewall and security group rules were authored for IPv4 only; author equivalent IPv6 rules or disable public IPv6 where it is not required
NAT gateways translate IPv6 automatically, so no action is needed
explain: Controls must be written for both address families; IPv6 rules were never created while public IPv6 addressing existed, so the fix is equivalent IPv6 policy or removing public IPv6 (C). IPv6 is filterable (A). Globally routable IPv6 addresses are public (B). NAT gateway behavior (D) does not govern native IPv6 routes.

q: An internal-only API sits behind an internal load balancer inside a VPC, yet compliance requires the same request inspection the public site gets. Where should its WAF be placed?
options: On each database instance
Attached to the internal load balancer fronting the API, inspecting east-west requests before they reach the services
A WAF cannot protect internal applications
At the internet edge only, even though the traffic never crosses it
explain: WAF placement follows the traffic path, not the internet: attaching it to the internal load balancer inspects API requests inline (C). (A) is false; WAFs work on internal load balancers. An edge WAF (B) never sees east-west traffic. Database instances (D) do not terminate the API's HTTP flows.

q: A single static VPN tunnel connects the data center to the production VPC, and every tunnel renegotiation briefly drops the payment link. Which design BEST improves resilience?
options: A spreadsheet documenting the outage windows
Longer IKE lifetimes on the single tunnel
A second tunnel with dynamic (BGP) routing across redundant customer gateways so failover is automatic
Moving payment traffic to the public internet permanently
explain: Redundant tunnels with BGP fail over automatically when one tunnel or gateway fails (D). Longer lifetimes (A) reduce renegotiation frequency but keep a single point of failure. Documentation (B) records, not prevents, outages. The public internet (C) abandons the private connectivity requirement.

q: A firm orders a dedicated private link to its cloud provider and tells auditors the traffic is 'private, therefore encrypted.' What must the security engineer correct and add?
options: The link should be replaced with public Wi-Fi for encryption
Only traffic volume needs monitoring
Dedicated links are private circuits but are not encrypted by default; add IPsec over the link or MACsec where supported to protect traffic in transit
Nothing; carrier links encrypt all traffic by default
explain: Dedicated connections such as direct cloud links provide a private path, not cryptographic protection; encryption must be layered with IPsec or MACsec (A). (B) states the misconception as fact. Public Wi-Fi (C) is absurd for this purpose. Monitoring volume (D) does not provide confidentiality.

q: An application tier inside a VNet must use a provider's managed storage platform. Leadership requires the traffic to arrive at the platform from an address inside the VNet's own address space so platform firewall rules can allow only that VNet. Which connectivity option fits?
options: A private endpoint, which places a network interface with a private address from the VNet inside the VNet for the platform service
An internet-facing VPN client on each application server
A public DNS alias for the storage account
A service endpoint, which keeps the platform's public address
explain: A private endpoint projects the managed service into the VNet as a private IP (D), enabling address-based platform firewall rules and keeping traffic off public addresses. A service endpoint (A) optimizes the route but the destination keeps a public address, failing the stated requirement. A DNS alias (B) changes names, not addressing. Per-server VPN clients (C) do not integrate the service into the VNet.

q: A hospital needs predictable latency and consistent bandwidth between its imaging center and its cloud archive, and regulators prohibit the traffic from traversing the public internet. Which option BEST fits?
options: A site-to-site VPN over the hospital's broadband line
A consumer file-sync service
A dedicated private connection ordered from a connectivity partner into the cloud provider
Port forwarding on the hospital firewall
explain: A dedicated private link gives deterministic performance and keeps traffic off the public internet (D). A VPN over broadband (A) still rides the public internet with variable performance. Port forwarding (B) exposes services rather than connecting networks. A file-sync service (C) is an application workaround, not private connectivity.

q: A SaaS provider must expose one application service privately to hundreds of customer VPCs, several of which use overlapping address ranges, without VPC peering to each customer. Which service model fits?
options: Full VPC peering with route renumbering for each customer
A public API with an IP allowlist
Site-to-site VPNs with NAT exceptions documented per customer
A private link-style service endpoint published by the provider and consumed as an endpoint inside each customer VPC
explain: Private link-style connectivity publishes a service as an endpoint inside each consumer VPC and tolerates overlapping consumer address space without peering (A). Peering (B) fails with overlapping ranges and does not scale. A public API (C) abandons private connectivity. VPN workarounds (D) multiply fragile per-customer exceptions.

q: Remote administrators connect over a VPN, but a split-tunnel configuration lets a compromised home machine reach the corporate cloud while simultaneously browsing untrusted networks. Which change BEST reduces this risk?
options: Use full-tunnel or posture-checked, per-application access so managed traffic cannot be bridged from untrusted networks through the admin machine
Increase VPN session length to a week
Allow split tunneling but ask users to be careful
Publish the admin portal publicly to remove the VPN
explain: Full tunneling or posture-validated per-app access prevents the endpoint from acting as an open bridge between untrusted networks and the cloud admin plane (B). Exhortation (A) is not a control. Week-long sessions (C) widen the exposure window. Publishing the portal (D) removes a layer of protection.

q: A new site-to-site VPN proposal from a partner suggests IKEv1 aggressive mode with a pre-shared key and weak Diffie-Hellman groups for 'compatibility.' What is the BEST security response?
options: Use the same pre-shared key for all partner tunnels
Disable encryption to speed up the tunnel
Accept it, because both ends support it
Require IKEv2 with strong encryption and modern Diffie-Hellman groups, preferring certificate authentication over shared keys
explain: Modern IKEv2 with strong suites and certificate authentication avoids the known weaknesses of aggressive mode, weak DH groups, and shared-key sprawl (C). Compatibility (A) does not excuse known-weak cryptography. Disabling encryption (B) defeats the tunnel's purpose. Reusing one key everywhere (D) makes one disclosure compromise every partner.

q: An enterprise is hardening its private connectivity into its main cloud region. Which TWO measures MOST improve assurance of that connectivity? (Choose two.)
options: Encrypt traffic over the dedicated link because the circuit alone does not provide confidentiality
Run redundant tunnels or paths with dynamic routing and alert on tunnel state changes
Use one tunnel and rely on the provider's marketing uptime figure
Share the VPN pre-shared key with all regional offices to simplify recovery
explain: Redundancy with dynamic routing and state alerting keeps private connectivity available and visible (A), and layering encryption onto the dedicated circuit corrects the false assumption that private means encrypted (C). A single tunnel (B) is a single point of failure. Shared pre-shared keys (D) turn one disclosure into a total compromise.

q: Policy requires all traffic between on-premises systems and cloud workloads, including traffic between two cloud subnets reached via the on-premises hub, to pass through the enterprise firewall for inspection. Which routing design enforces this?
options: Local internet breakout from each subnet
Forced tunneling that advertises a default route over the private connection so traffic hairpins through the on-premises firewall
Default VPC peering routes between the subnets
Direct public endpoints for every workload
explain: Forced tunneling with an advertised default route makes the on-premises firewall the transit point, so even cloud-to-cloud flows via the hub are inspected (A). Native peering routes (B) bypass the hub. Local breakout (C) and public endpoints (D) deliberately avoid central inspection.

q: A team creates a private endpoint for a managed database, but application servers still connect to the database's public address and fail its firewall checks. What is the MOST likely missing piece?
options: The database needs a larger instance size
The endpoint should be deleted so traffic uses the internet
Private DNS: the service name must resolve to the endpoint's private address through a private DNS zone linked to the VNet
The application servers need public IP addresses
explain: A private endpoint only helps if name resolution steers clients to it; without the linked private DNS zone, applications keep resolving the public address (C). Instance size (A) is unrelated. Public IPs on the servers (B) move traffic the wrong direction. Deleting the endpoint (D) abandons the private design rather than completing it.
