q: Tenants of a SaaS platform share one object store, separated only by key-name prefixes, and a flaw lets one tenant list and read objects under another tenant's prefix. Which control BEST restores isolation?
options: Move all objects into a single prefix so listing is uniform
Ask tenants to report objects that are not theirs
Enforce per-tenant authorization policies bound to the authenticated tenant identity on every object operation, ideally with per-tenant encryption keys
Rename prefixes to random strings
explain: Prefix naming is organization, not authorization; isolation requires the platform to authorize every request against the caller's tenant identity (D), with per-tenant keys adding cryptographic separation. Random names (A) are obscurity that listing already defeated. Tenant self-reporting (B) is not a control. A single prefix (C) removes even organizational separation.

q: A new enterprise customer will sign only if its virtual machines are guaranteed not to share physical hosts with any other customer, and it wants the guarantee in the architecture rather than a policy promise. Which offering satisfies this?
options: A shared host with a contractual penalty clause
Single-tenant dedicated hosts allocated exclusively to that customer
Stronger password rules for the hypervisor console
A larger shared cluster with more tenants for statistical safety
explain: Dedicated hosts make the customer the only tenant on the hardware, which is an architectural guarantee (C). Larger shared clusters (A) increase co-tenancy. Console passwords (B) protect management, not placement. A penalty clause (D) is a legal remedy, not the architectural guarantee requested.

q: When a tenant's virtual machine is destroyed, its virtual disk blocks are returned to the shared storage pool and later allocated to a different tenant. Which provider control protects the second tenant scenario in reverse, ensuring the first tenant's data is not readable?
options: Zeroing or cryptographic erasure of released blocks, or per-volume encryption whose keys are destroyed on release
Allocating blocks in strict alphabetical order
Defragmentation of the storage pool
Keeping destroyed tenants' disks for a year
explain: Released storage must be sanitized by overwriting or by destroying the volume's encryption key so residual data is unrecoverable by the next tenant (A). Defragmentation (B) reorganizes, not sanitizes. Retaining disks a year (C) prolongs exposure. Allocation order (D) has no sanitization effect.

q: On a shared host, one tenant's batch job consumes nearly all CPU for hours, and other tenants' latency breaches their service levels even though no security boundary was crossed. Which concept and control address this?
options: VM escape; patch the hypervisor
Data remanence; zero released disk blocks
Noisy neighbor; hypervisor resource shares, limits, and reservations per tenant
Cache timing; disable shared caches entirely
explain: This is the noisy neighbor problem (D): a resource fairness issue solved with shares, limits, and reservations, not a compromise. VM escape (A) involves breaking isolation, which did not occur. Remanence (B) concerns stored data after release. Cache timing (C) is a confidentiality side channel, not bulk CPU starvation.

q: A cloud provider's support model is being renegotiated by a regulated customer. Which TWO controls BEST limit provider-side access to the customer's tenant environment? (Choose two.)
options: Permanent standing admin accounts for provider engineers in every tenant
Full audit logging of any provider access session, visible to the customer
Just-in-time provider access that requires explicit customer approval (lockbox) before an engineer can enter the tenant
Giving the customer the provider's hypervisor source code
explain: Customer-gated just-in-time access removes standing privilege (B), and customer-visible audit logs make any approved access accountable (D). Standing provider accounts (A) are the exposure being negotiated away. Source code disclosure (C) is neither offered nor an access control for live tenant sessions.

q: A prospective tenant asks how it can gain confidence that a provider actually maintains tenant isolation, without being given other tenants' information. Which evidence is MOST appropriate?
options: Independent attestations such as SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 reports covering isolation controls, plus the provider's penetration-testing summaries
The provider's internal admin passwords, shared under NDA
The names of the provider's largest tenants
A tour where the tenant can watch other tenants' dashboards
explain: Independent audit reports and summarized test results evidence isolation controls without exposing any tenant (A). Other tenants' identities (B) and dashboards (C) would themselves violate isolation and confidentiality. Sharing admin credentials (D) destroys the control being evidenced.

q: A SaaS security team plans tenant-isolation testing before launch. Which test MOST directly probes the tenant boundary?
options: Checking that both tenants see the same login page
Load testing with simulated users from one tenant
Measuring page-load times for both tenants
Using tenant A's authenticated session to attempt reads, writes, and enumeration against tenant B's resource identifiers across the API and storage layers
explain: Deliberately attempting cross-tenant access with one tenant's credentials against the other's identifiers tests whether authorization enforces the boundary on every path (A). Load and timing tests (B, D) measure performance. A shared login page (C) is expected in multi-tenancy and proves nothing about data isolation.

q: A multi-tenant platform encrypts all tenant data with one shared key. A departing tenant demands provable destruction of its data, and counsel worries one key compromise exposes everyone. Which key architecture BEST resolves both concerns?
options: Store the shared key with each tenant
Keep the shared key but rotate it monthly
Two shared keys used on alternate days
Per-tenant encryption keys, so destroying a tenant's key cryptographically erases only that tenant's data and a single key compromise is contained
explain: Per-tenant keys align the cryptographic boundary with the tenant boundary: key destruction is per-tenant erasure, and compromise is scoped to one tenant (B). Rotating a shared key (A) cannot erase one tenant selectively and still exposes all tenants during any compromise window. Alternating shared keys (C) keeps the same blast radius. Giving tenants the shared key (D) hands everyone everyone's data.

q: A tenant running highly side-channel-sensitive cryptographic workloads accepts shared infrastructure for everything except this one system. Which mitigation BEST fits that system?
options: Place it on a dedicated host, and consider disabling simultaneous multithreading for that workload
Give its virtual machine the highest resource shares
Run it on the busiest shared hosts to hide in the crowd
Increase its network bandwidth allocation
explain: Side-channel exposure comes from sharing CPU resources, so a dedicated host and disabling simultaneous multithreading remove the co-resident observer (B). Busy shared hosts (A) maximize co-residency. Bandwidth (C) and resource shares (D) govern throughput and fairness, not microarchitectural leakage.

q: A company places each business unit's workloads in resource groups inside one cloud subscription, and an administrator's single mistaken role assignment grants a development team access to production resources across units. Which isolation boundary would have contained the mistake?
options: Longer resource names
Separate subscriptions or accounts per environment or unit, so role assignments and policy are scoped to that boundary
Tagging every resource with its owner's name
More resource groups inside the same subscription
explain: Subscriptions and accounts are the strong administrative isolation boundary: permissions granted inside one do not spill into another (D). Resource groups (A) organize resources but share the subscription's identity and policy plane, so the same mistake recurs. Names (B) and tags (C) are metadata, not authorization boundaries.

q: A risk assessment is cataloguing risks that arise specifically because infrastructure is multi-tenant rather than single-tenant. Which TWO belong in that catalogue? (Choose two.)
options: The provider's data center losing power to an entire facility
Co-residency side channels in which one tenant infers another tenant's activity from shared hardware behavior
A tenant's own employee misusing their legitimate access inside their own tenant
A misconfiguration granting one tenant access to another tenant's data or management functions
explain: Side channels exist only because tenants share hardware (B), and cross-tenant misconfiguration exposure exists only because a boundary between tenants must be enforced (C). Insider misuse within one's own tenant (A) occurs identically in single-tenant systems. A facility power loss (D) is an availability risk regardless of tenancy.

q: A provider notifies customers that a hypervisor flaw was found and fixed, with no evidence of exploitation, on hosts that ran multiple tenants. As a tenant security lead, what is the MOST prudent additional step for your most sensitive VMs?
options: Disable hypervisor logging in your own estate
Demand the names of the co-resident tenants
Terminate the account publicly before reading the report
Rotate credentials and keys that existed in guest memory on the affected hosts, and request the provider's attestation of patch completion
explain: If a hypervisor flaw could have exposed guest memory, rotating secrets that were resident and obtaining patch attestation is proportionate, evidence-based prudence (A). Co-tenant names (B) are irrelevant and properly withheld. Impulsive public termination (C) skips the facts. Disabling logging (D) reduces your own visibility for no benefit.

q: Customers of a retail site delivered through a CDN occasionally see another customer's personalized account page after signing in. The origin correctly marks those responses as private. What is the MOST likely CDN-side failure and fix?
options: The origin should mark account pages as publicly cacheable for an hour

The CDN cache is ignoring the origin's private/no-store directives or caching by an incomplete cache key; configure the CDN to honor cache-control for authenticated responses and vary the cache key correctly
The CDN is too geographically distributed; reduce its points of presence
Customers share IP addresses, so personalization is impossible
explain: Personalized responses must never enter a shared cache: a CDN that overrides private/no-store handling or keys cached objects without the authorization context will serve one customer another's page (A). Reducing points of presence (B) does not change cache semantics. Shared IP addresses (C) are normal and unrelated to cache keying. Marking account pages public (D) would guarantee the disclosure being investigated.

q: All traffic between subnets in a VPC is routed through one virtual firewall appliance in a single availability zone. When that zone is impaired, east-west inspection and connectivity fail together. Which redesign BEST removes this weakness?
options: Deploy redundant virtual firewall instances across availability zones with health-checked routing so inspection survives a zone loss
Give the single appliance a larger instance size
Accept the design because firewall appliances rarely fail
Remove the firewall and rely on security groups alone for all inspection
explain: A single inspection point in one zone is both a bottleneck and a single point of failure; redundant instances across zones with health-based route failover preserve inspection during a zone event (C). Accepting it (A) ignores a demonstrated architectural weakness. Security groups (B) filter coarsely but do not replace deep inspection where it is required. A larger single instance (D) is still one instance in one zone.

q: A provider markets a facility as concurrently maintainable, meaning any single capacity component can be removed for planned work without shutting down IT load. Which tier characteristic is this?
options: Tier II redundant capacity components only
A facility with no UPS requirement
Tier I basic capacity with a single distribution path
Tier III concurrently maintainable design
explain: Tier III requires concurrent maintainability plus redundant capacity, so planned maintenance needs no shutdown. Tier I has a single path and no redundancy. Tier II adds redundant components but still requires shutdown for distribution maintenance. That option is false for any rated tier.

q: During a site tour, an assessor finds a data hall cooled by two independent chillers where either chiller alone can carry the full critical load, plus a third identical unit. How is this cooling redundancy BEST described?
options: N+2, because two units are installed
2N with no spare capacity
N, because all units run at once
N+1, because one extra unit beyond the N needed is provided
explain: N+1 means N units meet the load and one additional unit provides redundancy if one fails or is maintained. 2N would require two complete independent systems each able to carry the full load. That option ignores the spare. That option would need two units beyond the required N.

q: A financial firm is shortlisting a new colocation site and rejects a location in a flood plain next to a chemical plant despite the lowest price. Which site-selection principle drove this decision?
options: Maximizing proximity to hazardous industry for shared utilities
Placing the facility where land-use rules prohibit data centers
Avoiding natural and man-made hazards that threaten long-term availability
Choosing the site with the lowest latency to headquarters regardless of hazards
explain: Site selection must weigh flood, seismic, weather, and neighboring hazards because a cheap site that floods or is evacuated destroys availability. Latency matters but does not override hazard exposure. That option increases risk. That option would make the site unusable, not safer.

q: Hot exhaust from one rack row is being drawn directly into the intakes of the facing row, raising inlet temperatures despite adequate total cooling capacity. Which control MOST directly fixes this?
options: Installing blanking panels only
Adding more CRAC units to the room
Implementing hot-aisle/cold-aisle containment
Raising the chilled-water setpoint
explain: Containment physically separates supply and exhaust air so cooling capacity is actually delivered to intakes. Raising setpoints worsens inlet temperatures. Blanking panels help within a rack but do not stop row-level mixing. More CRAC units add capacity without fixing distribution.

q: Failed drives containing regulated data are being placed in an unlocked bin for a vendor to collect monthly. Which facility media-handling practice BEST corrects this?
options: Store media in a locked, logged container and sanitize or destroy per NIST SP 800-88 before release, with chain of custody
Label drives as non-sensitive to speed vendor pickup
Overwrite drives once and return them to the spare pool without verification
Allow the vendor to sanitize media at its depot without documentation
explain: Secure media handling requires controlled storage, documented chain of custody, and verified sanitization or destruction before media leaves control. That option mislabels regulated data. That option surrenders control with no evidence. That option a single unverified overwrite is inadequate for regulated media leaving or re-entering use.

q: Which TWO controls are environmental protections for a cloud data center rather than logical access controls? (Choose two.)
options: VESDA very early smoke detection aspirating systems
SAML assertion signing for federated logins
Role-based access control on the cloud console
Water leak detection under raised floors with automated alerting
explain: VESDA detects smoke at incipient stages and leak detection catches water before it damages equipment; both are environmental controls. SAML signing and console RBAC are logical identity controls, not facility environmental protections.

q: A facility loses utility power. UPS batteries carry the load while generators start and synchronize, then generators carry the load for an extended outage. What is the PRIMARY role of the UPS in this sequence?
options: To cool the data hall during the outage
To replace generators for multi-day outages
To step utility voltage down for rack PDUs permanently
To provide immediate, conditioned bridging power until generator output is stable
explain: The UPS bridges the gap instantly and conditions power until generators are stable; its runtime is minutes, not days. That option reverses the roles. Cooling is a separate mechanical system, though it also needs backup power. That option describes transformation, not the bridging purpose tested here.

q: An operations manager proposes locating backup generators and fuel storage inside the same room as the primary electrical switchgear to save space. Why is this a POOR design?
options: Fuel cannot be stored indoors under any code
It creates a single point of failure where one fire or flood can disable both primary and backup power
Switchgear rooms are required to be unmanned at all times
Generators must always be on the roof
explain: Co-locating primary and backup power means a single incident can destroy both, defeating redundancy. That option is false; placement varies. That option is overstated; indoor storage is regulated, not universally banned. That option is not a code requirement and misses the resilience issue.

q: A provider claims 2N power distribution. During testing, maintenance on one complete power system forces an IT shutdown. What should the assessor conclude?
options: The facility should be reclassified as N+1 automatically
The design is truly 2N and shutdowns are expected
The as-built facility does not deliver true 2N, because either complete system should carry the full load alone
The test was invalid because 2N systems are never tested live
explain: True 2N means two fully independent systems, each capable of the entire load, so losing one never shuts down IT. If maintenance forces a shutdown, the claim is not met in practice. That option contradicts the definition. That option is false; live testing is expected. That option assumes a different design without evidence.

q: Which facility control MOST directly protects against unauthorized physical entry being undetected for hours in a cloud data center?
options: A mantrap with anti-tailgating controls, CCTV retention, and alarmed access points integrated with badge logs
Painting visitor areas a different color
Posting a guard roster on the lobby wall
Requiring visitors to sign a paper logbook only
explain: Layered physical detection and deterrence — mantraps, anti-tailgating, CCTV, and alarmed badge events — prevents and detects unauthorized entry. A paper logbook records only cooperative visitors and detects nothing. Those options provide no meaningful control.

q: Temperature sensors show a data hall within range at the CRAC return, but servers at the top of several racks are thermally throttling. What is the MOST likely infrastructure issue?
options: Humidity is necessarily too low
The facility tier is too high
The servers need faster CPUs
Return-air measurement is masking poor airflow distribution and hot spots at rack level
explain: A single return reading can hide stratification and recirculation that create rack-level hot spots; sensor placement at rack inlets is needed. That option ignores the thermal evidence. Humidity is not indicated by throttling alone. Tier describes redundancy design, not airflow distribution.

q: Which TWO statements about Tier IV fault-tolerant facilities are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Multiple independent, physically isolated distribution paths serve the load, with one active path model supported
Tier IV permits a single distribution path if UPS capacity is large
Fault tolerance eliminates the need for any maintenance planning
A single unplanned failure or disruption can be sustained without impact to critical load
explain: Tier IV is fault tolerant: compartmentalized, multiple independent paths sustain any single failure without load impact. That option is wrong because maintenance still requires planning even though it should not impact load. That option describes a lower tier; a single path cannot be fault tolerant.

q: A workforce IdP federates to a legacy enterprise SaaS app that only supports browser SSO with XML assertions and requires signed responses. Which federation protocol should the identity team implement?
options: OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant
SAML 2.0 Web Browser SSO
OpenID Connect with ID tokens
SCIM provisioning only
explain: The app's XML assertion and browser SSO requirement points to SAML 2.0. OIDC uses JWTs and JSON, which the app does not support. Client credentials is machine-to-machine authorization, not user SSO. SCIM provisions accounts; it does not authenticate users.

q: A mobile workforce app needs federated sign-in plus delegated API access using JSON-based tokens from the corporate IdP. Which combination BEST fits?
options: LDAP binds from the mobile app to the directory
OpenID Connect for authentication layered on OAuth 2.0 for delegated authorization
SAML 2.0 for both authentication and API delegation
Kerberos ticket exchange over the public internet
explain: OIDC on OAuth 2.0 is designed for JSON/JWT-based federation and delegated API access for modern apps. SAML is XML browser SSO and is not an API delegation framework. Kerberos is not suited to internet federation. Direct LDAP binds expose directory protocols and credentials.

q: Federated logins succeed, but an attacker replays a captured SAML assertion to a service provider a day later and gains access. Which validation failures MOST likely enabled this?
options: The IdP used SHA-256 instead of SHA-1
The SP requested NameID in email format
The SP did not enforce assertion expiry, audience restriction, and InResponseTo/one-time-use checks
Users were required to use MFA at the IdP
explain: Replay succeeds when the SP skips core SAML validation: Conditions/NotOnOrAfter, AudienceRestriction, and replay tracking. Stronger hashing would help, not hurt. MFA at the IdP does not validate a stolen assertion at the SP. NameID format is unrelated to replay.

q: An enterprise wants new hires to have cloud app accounts ready on day one and leavers' accounts disabled within minutes of HR termination, across dozens of SaaS apps. Which infrastructure capability is PRIMARY?
options: A shared spreadsheet of usernames updated weekly
Manual account creation by each app owner
Annual access recertification only
Automated identity provisioning and deprovisioning, typically via SCIM, driven by the authoritative HR source
explain: Automated lifecycle provisioning, commonly with SCIM and an authoritative source, creates and promptly removes accounts at scale. Manual creation and spreadsheets are slow and error-prone, especially for deprovisioning. Annual recertification detects stale access far too late.

q: MFA is enforced for the cloud console, but service accounts using long-lived passwords bypass it and one is compromised. What is the BEST infrastructure remediation?
options: Remove MFA from human accounts to equalize policy
Allow MFA bypass permanently for automation
Replace service-account passwords with workload identities, short-lived credentials, and conditional access that cannot bypass MFA-equivalent controls
Print service passwords and store them in a safe
explain: Workload identity with short-lived, scoped credentials removes the bypassable password path while preserving automation. Removing human MFA weakens security. Paper storage does not fix remote compromise or rotation. A permanent bypass is the vulnerability itself.

q: Which TWO measures strengthen a federation trust so a compromised or misconfigured partner IdP cannot silently assert any user in your cloud tenant? (Choose two.)
options: Require signed assertions and validate audience, issuer, and expiry on every response
Restrict accepted issuers and signing certificates, with pinned/rotated keys managed out of band
Accept unsigned assertions from any issuer that presents a matching email domain
Disable all federation logging to reduce noise
explain: Constraining trusted issuers and certificates and fully validating signed assertions bound what a partner can assert. Accepting unsigned assertions removes authentication of the assertion itself. Disabling logging destroys detection and accountability.

q: A company enforces phishing-resistant MFA for administrators but allows SMS codes for all other console users, and help-desk resets can downgrade any account to SMS. What is the WEAKEST link an attacker will target?
options: The FIDO2 keys used by administrators
The IdP's logo on the login page
The length of the console session timeout alone
The help-desk downgrade path and weaker SMS factor that undermine the stronger policy
explain: Attackers target the weakest authentication path; a reset process that downgrades to interceptable SMS defeats phishing-resistant MFA. The FIDO2 keys are the strongest element. Session length matters but is secondary. Branding is irrelevant.

q: In an OIDC flow, a relying party accepts an ID token without checking the nonce, issuer, or signature because the token arrived over TLS. Why is this unsafe?
options: Nonce checks are only required for SAML
TLS alone proves the token was issued for this client and this login attempt
TLS protects transport only; without signature, iss, aud, and nonce validation the app cannot prove authenticity, intended audience, or freshness of the token
ID tokens never need validation if they are JWTs
explain: OIDC validation is mandatory: signature proves authenticity, iss/aud prove it was meant for this app, and nonce binds it to the current request and resists replay. That option states the misconception. That option is false for any token format. That option reverses protocol requirements.

q: Directory synchronization is replicating all user attributes, including highly sensitive HR fields, to a cloud IdP that only needs name, email, and group membership. Which principle and fix apply?
options: Store the extra attributes in clear text for easier troubleshooting
Disable synchronization and create accounts manually
Apply attribute minimization: sync only the attributes the IdP and connected apps require
Synchronize more attributes to be safe for future use
explain: Attribute minimization limits breach impact and privacy exposure by syncing only what is needed. Syncing everything expands risk. Clear-text storage worsens exposure. Manual accounts sacrifice lifecycle automation when a scoped sync would work.

q: A federation metadata URL is fetched automatically every hour and trusts any new signing certificate published at that URL. What risk does this introduce, and what mitigates it?
options: If the metadata endpoint or DNS is compromised, an attacker can substitute a rogue signing key; mitigate with pinned trust anchors, change alerting, and controlled key rollover
The risk is only performance, mitigated by caching
The risk is user confusion, mitigated by training
No risk, because metadata is always trustworthy
explain: Auto-trusting fetched metadata makes the metadata channel itself a trust root; compromise lets an attacker inject a rogue IdP key, so pinning, alerting, and controlled rollover are required. That option is naive. Those options misidentify a trust-compromise risk as performance or awareness.

q: Contractors authenticate through a separate IdP domain federated to the same cloud tenant as employees, but contractor sessions receive the same default groups as staff. Which infrastructure change BEST enforces separation?
options: Remove MFA for contractors to distinguish their sessions
Rename contractor accounts with a prefix only
Give contractors employee groups for simpler administration
Use claims/attribute mapping and conditional access so the contractor issuer maps only to contractor-scoped groups and policies
explain: Issuer-aware claims mapping ensures the contractor trust only yields contractor permissions and policies. Granting staff groups is the problem. Removing MFA weakens security without creating separation. A naming prefix is cosmetic and enforces nothing.

q: Which TWO capabilities belong to identity provisioning infrastructure rather than authentication protocols? (Choose two.)
options: Joiner-mover-leaver workflows driven by an authoritative source such as HR
SCIM-based create, update, and deactivate operations against target applications
OIDC authorization code exchange at the token endpoint
SAML assertion consumption at the service provider
explain: SCIM lifecycle operations and joiner-mover-leaver workflows are provisioning: they create and maintain accounts. SAML consumption and OIDC code exchange are authentication-time protocol steps, not provisioning.

q: Engineers connect through a bastion host, but the bastion allows direct outbound internet access and stores administrators' private keys on its disk. Which statement BEST assesses this design?
options: It undermines the bastion model: a hardened, minimal jump point should have no stored credentials and tightly restricted egress, with keys held by users or a vault
It is acceptable because bastions are trusted by definition
Outbound access is required for SSH to work inbound
Private keys on a shared host improve accountability
explain: A bastion must be minimal and hardened; stored keys and open egress turn the single choke point into a high-value pivot. That option assumes trust instead of engineering it. That option confuses inbound session flow with unrestricted outbound access. That option destroys individual accountability.

q: A privileged access workstation program is being designed for cloud administrators. Which workstation profile is MOST appropriate?
options: A shared kiosk in the operations center with a common login
A dedicated, hardened workstation used only for privileged tasks, with no email or general web browsing, application allowlisting, and full-disk encryption
A general-purpose laptop used for email, browsing, and admin consoles
Any workstation as long as the browser is in private mode
explain: A PAW isolates privileged work from daily phishing and browsing risk through dedication and hardening. A dual-use laptop exposes admin credentials to commodity malware. Private browsing provides no meaningful isolation. A shared kiosk login destroys attribution.

q: A break-glass account was used during an outage, but no alert fired and the password was never rotated afterward. Which break-glass controls FAILED?
options: Monitoring/alerting on every break-glass use and mandatory credential rotation and review after use
The account existed at all
Requiring MFA for normal administrator accounts
Using a long password for the break-glass account
explain: Break-glass design depends on sealed credentials, immediate alerting, and post-use rotation and investigation. The account's existence is intentional for emergencies. Normal-account MFA is unrelated to this failure. Password length does not substitute for detection and rotation.

q: Cloud console access is allowed from any IP and any unmanaged device as long as the password and MFA succeed. Which additional infrastructure control BEST reduces session hijack and credential-theft risk?
options: Publishing a list of administrator usernames
Allowing console access through personal email recovery
Extending console session timeout to 30 days
Conditional access requiring compliant, managed devices and trusted locations or a secured admin network for console sign-in
explain: Device and network conditions bind console access to managed endpoints and expected paths, reducing the value of stolen credentials alone. Longer sessions increase hijack exposure. Email recovery adds a weaker path. Publishing usernames aids attackers.

q: An administrator's daily account, used for email, also holds permanent Owner rights in the production subscription, justified as 'faster during incidents.' What is the BEST correction?
options: Share the Owner account among on-call staff
Remove logging so elevation is faster
Separate daily and privileged accounts, with just-in-time elevation to Owner that is approved, time-bound, and logged
Keep permanent rights but require a stronger password
explain: Separating identities and using just-in-time elevation shrinks the window and blast radius of a compromised daily account while preserving incident access. A stronger password leaves standing privilege exposed to phishing. Removing logging and sharing accounts destroy accountability.

q: Which TWO design features make a jump-server deployment auditable and contained? (Choose two.)
options: Allowing administrators to bypass the jump host when they are in a hurry
Session recording with tamper-evident storage of privileged sessions
Network rules that allow target servers to accept administrative protocols only from the jump host
Copying all administrators' credentials onto the jump host for convenience
explain: Session recording provides evidence and source restriction forces traffic through the controlled path, together giving auditability and containment. A bypass defeats the choke point. Storing everyone's credentials creates a single high-value target.

q: After a contractor engagement ends, the contractor's bastion account is disabled, but their SSH key remains in authorized_keys on 40 servers. What went wrong?
options: Bastion accounts should never be disabled
Disabling the bastion account removes keys from all servers automatically
SSH keys expire automatically after 30 days by default
Access was not centrally managed: keys should be issued through a central authority or short-lived certificates so revoking the identity revokes access everywhere
explain: Direct per-server keys bypass central revocation; SSH certificates or centralized key management tie server access to identity lifecycle. That option is opposite of good practice. That option is false; standard OpenSSH keys do not expire by default. That option is false without automation that was clearly absent.

q: A cloud root console has MFA, but the MFA device is stored in the same safe as the written root password, accessible by one person alone. Which control principle is violated?
options: Least privilege
Separation of duties and dual control for the most privileged credentials
Defense in depth through more firewalls
Fail securely
explain: Storing both factors together under single-person control defeats MFA and dual control for the highest-privilege account. Least privilege concerns permission scope, not factor custody. Fail securely concerns failure defaults. More firewalls do not fix credential custody.

q: Operations wants administrators to reach private instances without a persistent bastion host exposed to the internet. Which modern alternative BEST meets this need?
options: Email private keys to administrators for direct connections
Use the cloud provider's managed session service that brokers authenticated, logged sessions to private instances with no inbound ports and no public IPs
Place all instances in public subnets
Open RDP on every instance to the internet
explain: A managed session broker provides authenticated, audited access to private resources without standing inbound exposure. Internet-open RDP and public subnets maximize attack surface. Emailing private keys breaks key custody and revocation.

q: A break-glass procedure requires two officers to retrieve sealed credentials from separate locations, and every use pages the security team. An auditor asks why so much friction is intentional. What is the BEST answer?
options: Break-glass access bypasses normal controls, so dual control, sealing, and alerting ensure it is rare, attributable, and investigated while still available in a true emergency
The procedure exists only to satisfy insurance paperwork
Friction is accidental and should be removed
Break-glass accounts are meant for routine daily administration
explain: Break-glass friction is deliberate: it keeps emergency bypass access available but ensures it cannot be used casually or secretly. That option misunderstands the design. Routine use would normalize bypassing controls. That option trivializes a real detective and deterrent control.

q: A new cloud account is created by a project team and left with default logging disabled, public storage allowed, and no password policy. Which baseline control would have prevented this at creation?
options: Asking the project team to read the security wiki
Running a penetration test a year later
Applying an account-level secure baseline automatically at provisioning through organization policies, guardrails, and infrastructure-as-code landing zone controls
Waiting for the annual audit to find the gaps
explain: A landing-zone baseline applies logging, storage, and identity guardrails automatically when an account, subscription, or project is created. Those options detect problems long after exposure. A wiki is advisory and unenforced.

q: A CIS Benchmark assessment finds a server deviates on audit log retention. The application owner says the benchmark setting breaks a legacy agent. What is the MOST appropriate handling?
options: Document a risk-based exception with compensating controls, an owner, and an expiry date, and track it in the baseline exception process
Disable the entire CIS Benchmark for all servers
Change the benchmark document to match the server
Silently ignore the deviation
explain: Mature baseline programs allow documented, time-bound exceptions with compensating controls rather than silent drift. Ignoring it hides risk. Disabling the benchmark fleet-wide is disproportionate. Editing the benchmark falsifies compliance evidence.

q: Golden images are rebuilt monthly, but running instances launched six months ago are never replaced and drift further from the current image each month. Which statement BEST describes the remaining risk?
options: Monthly rebuilds satisfy patch requirements for all instances regardless of age
There is no risk because the image library is current
The fleet's effective baseline is its running state, so stale instances retain old vulnerabilities and settings despite a current golden image
Golden images patch running instances automatically
explain: A current image only helps new launches; long-lived instances must be replaced or patched, otherwise their running state, not the library, defines real exposure.,, and all state the common misconception that image hygiene alone secures a running fleet.

q: A team applies a CIS Level 1 baseline to internet-facing production servers and a stricter Level 2 / STIG profile to servers handling regulated payment data. What does this demonstrate?
options: Risk-based tailoring of recognized benchmarks to system exposure and data sensitivity
Benchmarks are legally binding in their original form
Baselines should be identical for every system regardless of risk
Level 1 is always stricter than Level 2
explain: Tailoring recognized baselines by risk is expected practice: profile depth follows exposure and sensitivity. Identical baselines waste effort and can break low-risk systems or under-protect high-risk ones. Benchmarks are guidance unless adopted by regulation. That option reverses the levels.

q: Which TWO actions establish a trustworthy golden image pipeline? (Choose two.)
options: Manually log in to each new instance after launch to finish hardening
Allow any engineer to snapshot a manually configured server and publish it as golden without review
Record the image's provenance, benchmark version, and patch level so deployments are traceable
Build images from code in a controlled pipeline, scan and sign them, and promote only approved versions
explain: A controlled build with scanning, signing, and promotion plus recorded provenance makes images trustworthy and traceable. Ad-hoc snapshots import unknown state. Manual post-launch hardening reintroduces drift and inconsistency the image is meant to eliminate.

q: Configuration drift detection reports that 200 cloud storage buckets were changed outside the approved infrastructure-as-code pipeline overnight. What is the BEST first response from the platform security team?
options: Ignore the report because drift is normal
Identify the changes and their source, assess whether any bucket became public or lost logging/encryption, and contain exposed resources before reconciling with the pipeline
Re-run the pipeline to overwrite everything without investigation
Immediately delete all 200 buckets
explain: Drift may signal compromise or error, so the team must first understand scope and exposure and contain public or unprotected resources before overwriting evidence or state. Blind deletion destroys data. Ignoring it accepts unknown exposure. Blind re-application can destroy forensic evidence and legitimate emergency changes.

q: A cloud organization policy denies public IP assignment by default, but a team requests an exception for a single jump host project. How should this baseline guardrail be implemented?
options: Remove the organization policy for everyone
Grant a narrowly scoped, time-bound exception at the specific project/resource level with logging and review, leaving the deny-by-default guardrail intact
Give the team organization administrator rights to self-approve
Disable policy evaluation in audit mode permanently
explain: Scoped exceptions preserve the guardrail while enabling a justified need with accountability. Removing the policy exposes every project. Permanent audit-only mode makes the policy decorative. Self-approval via org admin violates separation of duties and least privilege.

q: Before a hardened image is promoted, automated checks confirm unnecessary services are disabled, host firewall defaults to deny, and logging agents are present. Which phase of baseline management is this?
options: Post-incident forensics
Decommissioning
User acceptance testing of business features
Baseline validation against the defined secure configuration before release
explain: Pre-release validation verifies the image actually matches the intended baseline before it becomes the fleet standard. Forensics is after an incident. Business UAT tests application function, not hardening. Decommissioning is end of life.

q: A subscription baseline requires diagnostic logs to flow to a central, immutable log store. A team routes its logs to a local storage account it controls and can delete. Why does this fail the baseline's intent?
options: Central logging is only about saving storage costs
Local storage is always slower
Logs under the control of the team being monitored can be altered or deleted by that team, breaking tamper evidence and central detection
The baseline requires logs to be printed and archived
explain: Separation between log producers and log custody is the point: immutable central storage prevents a compromised or malicious team account from erasing evidence. Cost and speed are not the security intent. Printing logs is not a cloud baseline requirement.

q: An organization adopts CIS Benchmarks but discovers its images also need a vendor-specific database service disabled that CIS does not cover. What should the team do?
options: Wait for CIS to publish an update before acting
Layer an organization-specific baseline on top of CIS, documenting the additional requirements in the internal standard
Enable the database service because CIS is silent on it
Abandon CIS because it is incomplete
explain: Benchmarks are a floor, not a ceiling; organizations add their own requirements for risks the benchmark does not address. Abandoning CIS loses broad value. Treating silence as permission leaves a known exposure. Waiting delays a known fix indefinitely.

q: A platform team measures baseline compliance at 98 percent, but the noncompliant 2 percent includes every domain controller-equivalent identity server. How should a CCSP interpret this metric?
options: Compliance should be measured only by counting servers
The metric proves the baseline itself is wrong
Aggregate percentages hide criticality: noncompliance on the highest-value assets can represent the majority of actual risk and must be prioritized
98 percent is excellent, so no action is needed
explain: Risk is not evenly distributed; identity infrastructure is a top attacker target, so its noncompliance outweighs a high fleet average. That option is complacency driven by a vanity metric. That option does not follow from the data. That option is exactly the counting flaw being criticized.

q: A vulnerability scan reports a critical, internet-exploitable flaw on a public-facing cloud workload, while a second critical flaw sits on an isolated build server with no network path. Which should be patched FIRST, and why?
options: The internet-facing workload, because exploitability and exposure, not CVSS score alone, drive prioritization
Neither, because both have the same CVSS score
The build server, because it was scanned first
Both can wait for the quarterly window
explain: Prioritization combines severity with exposure and exploitability; an internet-reachable critical flaw is imminently exploitable. Scan order is arbitrary. Waiting ignores active risk. Identical CVSS is precisely why context must supplement the score.

q: A vendor releases an emergency patch for a flaw being actively exploited in cloud management interfaces. The normal change window is in three weeks. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Use the expedited/emergency change path with focused testing, staged deployment, and rollback plan to patch promptly
Disable change management permanently
Wait for the normal window to avoid process violations
Patch production without any testing or record
explain: Emergency change processes exist for actively exploited flaws: faster, but still tested, staged, documented, and reversible. Waiting three weeks leaves a known exploited hole. Patching with no test or record trades one risk for chaos. That option destroys governance for a single event.

q: Agent-based scanning misses short-lived containers that exist for only minutes, so a vulnerable image runs repeatedly without ever being scanned. Which approach BEST closes this gap?
options: Scan the environment monthly instead of weekly
Extend container lifetimes so scanners can catch them
Rely on developers to report vulnerabilities in their containers
Shift scanning left to the image/registry and pipeline, blocking vulnerable images from deployment, supplemented by runtime visibility
explain: Scanning and gating images before deployment covers ephemeral workloads that agents cannot reliably reach. Less frequent scanning widens the gap. Self-reporting is unreliable. Extending lifetimes defeats the architecture to suit the tool.

q: Which TWO metrics together give leadership a truthful picture of patch program health? (Choose two.)
options: Total number of patches installed, with no severity or asset context
Percentage of in-scope assets covered by scanning, so unscanned systems are visible as risk
Number of vulnerability scan licenses purchased
Mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities on internet-facing assets, trended over time
explain: Time-to-remediate for critical exposed flaws and scan coverage together show speed and blind spots. Raw patch counts reward volume over risk reduction. License counts measure purchasing, not security outcomes.

q: A patch repeatedly fails on a legacy server that cannot be rebooted until year-end, and the flaw is remotely exploitable. Which compensating approach is MOST appropriate in the interim?
options: Mark the vulnerability as a false positive to close the ticket
Apply virtual patching / IPS or WAF rules and network isolation that block exploitation of the specific flaw, with a documented expiry tied to the patch date
Lower the vulnerability's severity in the scanner
Do nothing until the reboot is possible
explain: Virtual patching plus isolation reduces exploitability while the real patch is deferred under documented risk acceptance. Doing nothing leaves an exploitable hole. Falsifying status or severity corrupts risk data without reducing risk.

q: Authenticated (credentialed) scans are replaced with unauthenticated scans to 'reduce risk' of using scanner credentials. What is the main consequence?
options: Unauthenticated scans find more vulnerabilities
Scan results lose depth and accuracy: missing patches and local misconfigurations go undetected and false confidence increases, unless scanner credentials are vaulted and tightly controlled
Unauthenticated scans patch systems automatically
Scanner credentials are never needed for cloud workloads
explain: Credentialed scanning sees installed patches and local configuration that a network-only view cannot; the right control is vaulting and scoping scanner credentials, not blinding the scanner. That option reverses reality. That option is false for OS-level assessment. That option confuses scanning with remediation.

q: A cloud workload is built from infrastructure as code, and a critical OS patch is released. The team patches the running instance by hand but does not update the code or golden image. What will happen?
options: Future instances launched from the unchanged code/image will reintroduce the vulnerability, so the patch must be made in the source artifact
The fix persists across all future deployments
Nothing, because running instances are the only ones that matter
Hand patching updates the image automatically
explain: In IaC and image-based fleets, durable fixes belong in the source artifact; a hand patch dies with the instance and the flaw returns at next launch. Those options state the misconception. That option ignores that fleets are constantly relaunched and scaled.

q: A scanner flags a high-severity CVE in a software library that is present in an image but is never loaded or executed by the application, with no exploitable path. How should a mature program handle this?
options: Treat it identically to an exploitable flaw and halt all releases indefinitely
Delete the finding so metrics improve
Record a risk-based disposition with reachability analysis, monitor for changes, and prioritize exploitable instances first while planning the library upgrade
Ignore all library vulnerabilities in the future
explain: Reachability-aware triage focuses effort on exploitable risk while keeping the finding documented and revisited, rather than freezing delivery or corrupting data. That option misallocates scarce patch capacity. That option falsifies metrics. That option generalizes one disposition into negligence.

q: Patch compliance is enforced by auto-terminating any instance older than 30 days and forcing relaunch from the current golden image. Which prerequisite makes this SAFE for production?
options: Instances must hold unique, irreplaceable local state
Users should be given no notice and no rollback image kept
Workloads must be stateless or externalize state, with health checks and graceful connection draining so replacement does not cause data loss or outages
Termination should happen at peak traffic for faster turnover
explain: Forced replacement is safe only when state is externalized and replacement is health-gated and drained. Irreplaceable local state is exactly what makes auto-termination dangerous. Peak-time termination maximizes impact. No rollback removes recovery options.

q: Employees access a sanctioned SaaS app through their browsers, and the security team needs inline inspection and session controls as traffic flows through a proxy the company operates. Which CASB mode is this?
options: Reverse-proxy CASB
API-based CASB
Forward-proxy CASB
Log-based discovery only
explain: A forward proxy sits in the user-to-cloud path, typically via endpoint agent or PAC, giving inline visibility and control for traffic to sanctioned and unsanctioned apps. API mode is out-of-band. Reverse proxy sits in front of a specific app, usually for unmanaged devices. Log discovery only identifies app usage.

q: A company needs data-at-rest scanning, sharing analysis, and compliance reports inside a sanctioned SaaS tenant, including activity that happened before the CASB was purchased. Which CASB mode BEST provides this?
options: Forward proxy, because it sees historical stored data
Reverse proxy, because it rewrites app URLs
DNS filtering only
API-based CASB, because it connects to the SaaS provider's APIs to scan stored content and audit configuration and sharing, including retrospectively
explain: API-based CASB queries the provider directly, so it can scan existing stored data, permissions, and configuration out-of-band. A forward proxy sees only traffic passing through it after deployment. Reverse proxy is inline for sessions, not historical storage. DNS filtering cannot inspect SaaS content.

q: Unmanaged contractor laptops must access an internal web app through the CASB with MFA and device-posture checks, without installing an agent. Which mode fits BEST?
options: Reverse-proxy CASB, which brokers the session to the app and can enforce access and session controls without an endpoint agent
Offline log analysis
Forward proxy with a mandatory endpoint agent
API-based scanning of the app database
explain: Reverse proxy inserts the CASB in front of the application, ideal for unmanaged/BYOD access where agents cannot be installed. Forward proxy contradicts the no-agent constraint. API mode does not broker live sessions. Log analysis is detective and after the fact.

q: A SASE rollout replaces site VPN backhauling: branch users connect to the nearest provider point of presence for secure web gateway, CASB, and zero-trust access enforcement. What is the PRIMARY architectural benefit?
options: SASE eliminates the need for identity controls
Security inspection moves to cloud-delivered points of presence near users, improving performance while applying consistent policy wherever users work
SASE is only a marketing term for a firewall refresh
All traffic must still hairpin through headquarters
explain: SASE converges networking and security at distributed cloud edges, avoiding backhaul latency while keeping policy consistent. Hairpinning is what SASE removes. Identity remains central — SASE/ZTNA depends on it. That option dismisses a real architectural shift.

q: Shadow IT discovery shows staff using an unsanctioned file-sharing service. Leadership wants coaching and control rather than an immediate hard block that would break a client deadline. Which CASB capability BEST supports this?
options: Block all cloud storage including the sanctioned platform

Use CASB risk ratings and policy controls to permit the app with restrictions such as blocking uploads of sensitive data, applying user coaching pages, and monitoring use while a sanctioned alternative is adopted
Permanently allow the app with no controls
Disable discovery reporting so leadership is not alarmed
explain: CASB enables graduated control: app risk context, DLP on uploads, and coaching steer users without an abrupt block. Unconditional allowance accepts the risk silently. Suppressing reports hides it. Blocking everything punishes sanctioned use and drives more shadow IT.

q: Which TWO statements correctly contrast CASB deployment modes? (Choose two.)
options: Reverse proxy is the best tool for scanning data at rest historically stored in SaaS
API-based mode can block a user's keystroke in real time
Forward proxy provides inline control for traffic routed through it but requires traffic steering such as an agent or PAC file
API-based mode provides out-of-band visibility into sanctioned apps without sitting inline in user traffic
explain: Forward proxy is inline and needs steering, and API mode is out-of-band against sanctioned apps — both correct. Reverse proxy brokers sessions; historical at-rest scanning is API mode's strength. That option is false because out-of-band API controls cannot act in real time inline.

q: In a SASE/ZTNA design, a user passes MFA yet is denied access to a finance application from a jailbroken phone on an untrusted network. Which principle explains the denial?
options: Once authenticated, users receive broad network access
ZTNA continuously evaluates identity, device posture, and context per application, so a failed posture check denies that app even with valid MFA
MFA failure is the only possible cause of denial
ZTNA grants access based on network location alone
explain: Per-app, context-aware authorization means authentication is necessary but not sufficient; device posture and risk signals gate each application. That option describes old perimeter VPN thinking. That option ignores posture evaluation. That option describes flat network access that ZTNA is designed to replace.

q: A CASB in forward-proxy mode cannot inspect a SaaS app's traffic because the app uses certificate pinning on mobile clients. What is the BEST complementary control?
options: Block the mobile app store
Disable certificate pinning guidance and intercept anyway
Pair the proxy with API-based CASB for that sanctioned app to gain visibility into content and sharing through the provider's APIs
Abandon all CASB controls for that app
explain: When pinning defeats inline TLS inspection, API-based CASB restores visibility out-of-band for sanctioned apps. Forcing interception breaks the app and its security design. Abandoning control leaves a blind spot unaddressed. That option is irrelevant to the visibility problem.

q: A cloud root account is used weekly by the platform lead for routine billing changes and support plan updates. Which change BEST aligns with root-account protection guidance?
options: Share root credentials with the whole platform team for coverage
Keep using root but choose a longer password
Lock down root with strong MFA, remove its access keys, and perform daily work through federated administrative roles, reserving root only for the few tasks that truly require it
Disable MFA on root to avoid lockout during emergencies
explain: Root should be vaulted and almost never used: MFA protected, no access keys, with routine work done via least-privilege federated roles. A longer password does not fix routine use of an unrestricted account. Sharing destroys attribution. Disabling MFA invites takeover of the entire account.

q: Long-lived cloud API access keys for the CI system were found committed to a public code repository eight months ago and are still active. What is the CORRECT response sequence?
options: Delete the repository file and assume the keys are safe
Treat the keys as compromised: revoke/rotate them immediately, review usage logs for unauthorized activity across the exposure window, and replace them with short-lived workload credentials
Rename the keys so attackers cannot find them
Wait for the provider to detect abuse
explain: Publicly exposed keys must be assumed compromised: immediate revocation, log review for the full window, and migration to short-lived credentials. Deleting the file does not un-expose copied keys. Renaming does nothing; keys are values, not names. Waiting cedes the response to the provider.

q: Which TWO controls BEST protect infrastructure API credentials in a mature cloud environment? (Choose two.)
options: Prefer temporary, automatically rotated credentials from instance/workload roles over static access keys
Store static keys in a managed secrets vault with access logging, rotation, and least-privilege scoping when they cannot be eliminated
Embed keys in container images for reliable deployment
Grant each key full administrator rights to avoid permission errors
explain: Temporary workload credentials shrink exposure windows, and vaulted, logged, rotated, scoped keys control the static keys that remain. Embedding keys in images spreads them to every registry and runner. Full admin keys maximize blast radius.

q: An attacker gains a developer's cloud API key that has permissions to create new IAM users and attach policies. Even though no data is directly readable with the key, why is this still a CRITICAL management-plane compromise?
options: Privilege-escalation permissions let the attacker mint persistent administrative identities, so the key is effectively a path to full account takeover
It is not critical until data is read
Creating users is a harmless administrative function
API keys cannot be used outside business hours
explain: Management-plane permissions that create or modify identities convert a single leaked key into durable, full control, independent of direct data access. That option understates escalation risk. That option is false; keys work around the clock. That option ignores that user creation is the core of account administration.

q: A provider's management console and APIs are reachable from the public internet with only password authentication for a legacy support account that bypasses the corporate IdP. What is the priority fix?
options: Change the console theme to warn users
Allow the bypass because support accounts are low risk
Bring all management-plane access under federated SSO with MFA, or disable the local legacy account, so no path bypasses central identity policy
Add the account to the password rotation spreadsheet
explain: Any management-plane path that bypasses federation and MFA is an unmonitored back door and must be closed or integrated. A spreadsheet does not add authentication strength. A warning theme is cosmetic. Support accounts often hold high privilege and are prime targets.

q: Root account recovery depends on an email inbox and phone number controlled by a former employee's personal accounts. Why is this a management-plane emergency, and what fixes it?
options: Root recovery is disabled in all cloud accounts by default
Whoever controls root recovery channels can reset the ultimate credentials, so recovery contacts must be moved to company-controlled, monitored email and phone under dual control
It is only an HR issue with no security impact
Changing the root password daily eliminates recovery risk
explain: Account recovery is an authentication path to root; personal, ex-employee-controlled channels mean an outsider may retain a route to full account takeover, so channels must be corporate, monitored, and dual-controlled. That option denies the technical impact. That option is false. Daily password changes do not fix who can reset it.

q: A team wants to find SQL injection by analyzing source code before the application ever runs. Which testing type fits, and when does it occur?
options: RASP, at deployment time
SCA, on third-party licenses
SAST (white-box), early in the SDLC on source/bytecode
DAST, during production monitoring
explain: SAST (B) analyzes source or bytecode without executing it, early and shift-left. DAST (A) is wrong because it tests running applications as a black box. RASP (C) is wrong because it protects at runtime in production. SCA (D) is wrong because it analyzes third-party component composition, not custom code flaws.

q: A QA team deploys an agent inside the test application that observes code execution during functional tests and reports the exact vulnerable lines. Which testing type is this?
options: DAST
IAST
SAST
Manual code review
explain: IAST (A) instruments the running application with agents, combining runtime observation with code-level detail during tests. SAST (B) is wrong because it never executes code. DAST (C) is wrong because it tests externally with no code visibility. Manual review (D) is wrong because it is human-driven, not agent-instrumented.

q: After a critical OpenSSL CVE is announced, a CISO needs a list of every product embedding the vulnerable version. Which capability provides this?
options: SCA with an SBOM inventory
DAST
Fuzzing
SAST
explain: SCA inventories third-party and open-source components, and an SBOM maps exactly which products embed which versions (D). SAST (A) is wrong because it analyzes custom source, not component inventory. DAST (B) is wrong because it tests running behavior. Fuzzing (C) is wrong because it finds crashes, not component lists.

q: A company wants protection that lives inside the application runtime and blocks exploits in production without signature updates. Which technology fits?
options: WAF
Network IDS
RASP
SAST
explain: RASP (C) instruments the application runtime to detect and block attacks in real time without signature updates. SAST (A) is wrong because it is pre-deployment static analysis. A WAF (B) is wrong because it sits in front of the app at the network edge. Network IDS (D) is wrong because it monitors traffic, not in-process execution.

q: A web app needs users to log in with their cloud identity and grant the app limited API access without sharing passwords. Which OAuth 2.0 flow is MOST appropriate?
options: Resource owner password credentials
Implicit flow
Authorization code flow (with PKCE)
Client credentials flow
explain: The authorization code flow with PKCE (B) is the secure standard for user-delegated access without exposing credentials. Client credentials (A) is wrong because it is for machine-to-machine scenarios, not users. The implicit flow (C) is wrong because it is deprecated and exposes tokens in URLs. Password credentials (D) is wrong because it requires sharing the user's password.

q: An application needs to authenticate users via an identity provider and receive a signed token asserting who the user is. Which standard provides this identity layer?
options: OpenID Connect, using ID tokens (JWTs) on top of OAuth 2.0
LDAP bind
SAML 1.0 over email
Basic authentication
explain: OpenID Connect (A) adds an identity layer to OAuth 2.0 with signed JWT ID tokens asserting the user's identity. SAML 1.0 (B) is wrong because it is outdated, and OIDC is the modern identity layer. Basic authentication (C) is wrong because it sends credentials with every request. LDAP bind (D) is wrong because it is a directory protocol, not a federated identity layer.

q: Two organizations need browser-based SSO where the identity provider sends XML assertions about the user to the service provider. Which standard is this?
options: OAuth 2.0 alone
SCIM
OpenID Connect
SAML 2.0
explain: SAML 2.0 (D) uses XML assertions exchanged between the identity provider and service provider for federated SSO. OAuth 2.0 alone (A) is wrong because it is an authorization framework, not federated authentication assertions. OpenID Connect (B) is wrong because it uses JSON/JWT tokens, not XML assertions. SCIM (C) is wrong because it provisions identities rather than asserting authentication.

q: A company exposes 200 microservice APIs and needs centralized authentication, rate limiting, and usage analytics. Which component BEST provides this?
options: A database firewall
An API gateway
Direct client-to-service connections
A code obfuscator
explain: An API gateway (C) centralizes authentication, throttling and rate limiting, and usage analytics at the edge. A database firewall (A) is wrong because it protects databases, not APIs. Direct connections (B) are wrong because they scatter policy enforcement across services. Obfuscation (D) is wrong because it hides code rather than managing APIs.

q: A hospital needs access decisions based on user role PLUS department, shift time, and patient relationship. Which model fits BEST, and why?
options: DAC, because owners decide everything
MAC, because labels are mandatory
ABAC, because it evaluates multiple attributes against policies
RBAC, because roles alone handle time-based rules
explain: ABAC (A) evaluates attributes such as role, department, time, and relationship against policy, which is far more expressive than roles alone. RBAC (B) is wrong because roles alone cannot express time or context conditions. DAC (C) is wrong because owner discretion does not scale to contextual policies. MAC (D) is wrong because it uses fixed clearance labels, not dynamic attributes.

q: A developer commits a cloud secret key to a public repository. What is the FIRST correct response?
options: Revoke/rotate the exposed secret immediately and scan for misuse
Delete the commit and assume the key is safe
Rotate the developer's laptop password
Add the key to the README for visibility
explain: Exposed secrets must be revoked and rotated at once, with usage audited for misuse (D), because deletion does not un-expose them. (A) is wrong because copies persist in clones and history. (B) is wrong because the laptop password is unrelated to the exposed key. (C) is obviously wrong.

q: A build pulls 'reqeusts' instead of 'requests' from a public registry, installing malware. Which controls BEST prevent recurrence?
options: Disabling the firewall
Dependency pinning, private registries, and SCA scanning for typosquatting
More unit tests
Longer passwords
explain: Pinning versions, using curated private registries, and SCA detection (B) counter typosquatting and dependency confusion. Unit tests (A) are wrong because they do not vet package provenance. Passwords (C) are wrong and unrelated. (D) is wrong and actively harmful.

q: Which is the BEST practice for application secrets in cloud workloads?
options: Hardcode them in source for reliability
Central vault with dynamic short-lived credentials, rotation, and audit logging
Store them in environment variables on shared servers with no rotation
Email them to the team for backup
explain: A vault issuing short-lived dynamic secrets with rotation and auditing (C) is the standard. (A) exposes secrets to every repository reader. (B) leaves long-lived secrets unrotated on shared hosts. (D) exposes secrets in mail stores.

q: Which control is MOST effective at blocking SQL injection and XSS attempts against a cloud web application at the edge?
options: Antivirus on the web server
WAF with OWASP core rule set
Full-disk encryption
Network firewall ACLs
explain: A WAF (A) inspects HTTP-layer payloads against attack signatures for SQL injection and XSS. Network ACLs (B) are wrong because they filter IPs and ports, not payloads. Antivirus (C) is wrong because it targets malware, not web exploits. Disk encryption (D) is wrong because it protects data at rest.

q: A team integrates SAST, SCA, and DAST into the CI/CD pipeline so every commit is security-tested automatically. Which practice does this BEST represent?
options: Manual penetration testing
DevSecOps / shift-left security
Big-bang deployment
Waterfall development
explain: Embedding automated security testing throughout CI/CD (D) is DevSecOps shift-left. Waterfall (A) is wrong because it sequences phases with late testing. Manual penetration testing (B) is wrong because it is periodic and human-driven. Big-bang deployment (C) is wrong because it describes deployment style, not security integration.

q: A cloud-native app must run identically in dev, staging, and prod with no code changes. Which 12-factor principle MOST directly enables this?
options: Hardcode backing services as localhost
Run admin tasks manually on servers
Store logs on local disk
Store config in the environment, strictly separating config from code
explain: Externalized configuration via environment variables (B) keeps one codebase deployable across environments with no code changes. Local disk logs (A) is wrong because 12-factor treats logs as event streams. Manual admin tasks (C) is wrong because one-off processes should run in identical environments. Hardcoded services (D) is wrong because backing services must be attached resources.

q: A cloud storage bucket is created private with no public access, requiring explicit action to share. Which principle does this demonstrate?
options: Least common mechanism
Security through obscurity
Secure defaults (deny by default)
Open design
explain: Deny-by-default with explicit opt-in to sharing (C) is secure defaults. Obscurity (A) is wrong because the control is real access enforcement, not hiddenness. Open design (B) is wrong because it concerns public algorithms, not defaults. Least common mechanism (D) is wrong because it concerns shared components.

q: A company buys a third-party web application as compiled binaries with no source code, and wants to find runtime vulnerabilities like injection flaws before production. Which testing type fits?
options: SAST
IAST
SCA
DAST
explain: DAST (B) tests a running application from the outside with no source access — exactly the black-box situation with a third-party product. SAST (A) analyzes source code, which is unavailable. IAST (C) needs an agent deployed inside the app during testing. SCA (D) inventories open-source components, not runtime vulnerabilities.

q: After a legal review flags copyleft-licensed code inside a commercial SaaS product, the CISO wants automated detection of risky open-source licenses in every build. Which capability provides this?
options: SCA
DAST
RASP
SAST
explain: Software Composition Analysis (A) inventories third-party and open-source components and flags both known CVEs and license risks such as copyleft GPL code in a commercial product. DAST (B) tests running apps for runtime flaws. RASP (C) protects apps at runtime. SAST (D) analyzes first-party source code, not dependency licenses.

q: A user discovers that changing the order number in a URL from /orders/1042 to /orders/1043 displays another customer's order details. Which OWASP Top 10 category is this?
options: Cross-site scripting
Security misconfiguration
Broken access control
Injection
explain: Changing an object ID in a URL to access another user's data is broken access control (C) — specifically insecure direct object reference (IDOR): the app fails to verify the requester owns the object. Injection (A) executes malicious commands or queries. XSS (B) runs scripts in another user's browser. Security misconfiguration (D) covers defaults and error handling, not authorization logic.

q: A mobile API endpoint /api/v1/accounts/{id} returns any account's details when the ID is changed, with no ownership check. Which API-specific vulnerability is this?
options: JWT algorithm confusion
Rate limiting
Broken object level authorization
Mass assignment
explain: Broken object level authorization (D) — the API Security Top 10's leading risk — is failing to verify that the caller is authorized for the specific object requested. Rate limiting (A) throttles abuse but does not fix authorization. JWT algorithm confusion (B) is an authentication flaw, not object authorization. Mass assignment (C) binds unexpected input fields, a different issue.

q: An API accepts JWTs from an identity provider. Which validation approach is MOST secure?
options: Store tokens in localStorage and trust the client
Skip expiry checks for better user experience
Accept any JWT as long as it is well-formed
Validate the signature, expiry, issuer, and reject tokens using 'none'
explain: Secure JWT handling (A) requires verifying the cryptographic signature with the issuer's key, checking expiry and issuer claims, and rejecting the 'none' algorithm that disables signatures. Accepting well-formed tokens (B) trusts attacker-forged claims. Client-side storage trust (C) and skipping expiry (D) both remove essential validation.

q: A native mobile app needs users to authenticate with a cloud identity provider and authorize the app for limited API scopes, without the app ever seeing the password. Which OAuth2 flow should it use?
options: OAuth2 authorization code flow with PKCE
OAuth2 resource owner password credentials flow
OAuth2 implicit flow
OAuth2 client credentials flow
explain: Authorization code with PKCE (B) is the current best practice for mobile/public clients: the code is exchanged securely and PKCE prevents authorization-code interception. The implicit flow (A) is deprecated because tokens pass through the browser. The password flow (C) requires handling raw user credentials. Client credentials (D) is for service-to-service auth with no user involved.

q: A single-page application needs both delegated API access AND a signed assertion of the user's identity from the identity provider. Which standard provides both?
options: SAML, which is designed for APIs
OAuth2, which authenticates users directly
OpenID Connect, which adds an identity layer on OAuth2
LDAP, which issues ID tokens
explain: OpenID Connect (C) is the identity layer built on OAuth2 — it adds the ID token asserting who the user is. OAuth2 alone (A) authorizes API access but does not authenticate the user. SAML (B) is for browser-based SSO, not modern API/mobile flows. LDAP (D) is a directory protocol that does not issue ID tokens.

q: A web application uses long-lived sessions via refresh tokens. Which handling BEST limits the damage if a refresh token is stolen?
options: Rotate refresh tokens and revoke them on logout
Allow unlimited refresh token reuse
Pass refresh tokens in URLs
Never expire refresh tokens
explain: Rotating refresh tokens (each use issues a new one and invalidates the old) plus revocation on logout (D) limits the window a stolen token is useful. Non-expiring tokens (A) and unlimited reuse (C) maximize attacker value. Tokens in URLs (B) leak via logs, history, and referers.

q: A microservices platform has 40 service accounts calling each other's APIs. Which access approach BEST limits blast radius if one service is compromised?
options: One shared admin account for all services
RBAC with least-privilege roles for each service account
ABAC is always required instead of RBAC
No authentication between internal services
explain: RBAC with least-privilege roles (A) gives each service account only the permissions its function needs — the standard control for machine identities. A shared admin account (B) violates least privilege and destroys attribution. ABAC (C) is powerful but not mandatory; RBAC fits stable service roles well. Unauthenticated internal traffic (D) enables lateral movement.

q: After a credential-phishing incident, a company wants a second factor that cannot be phished or SIM-swapped. Which option BEST meets this?
options: Email one-time passcodes
SMS one-time passcodes
FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware security keys
Security questions
explain: FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys (B) are phishing-resistant: the private key never leaves the device and authentication is bound to the legitimate origin, defeating credential phishing and SIM swapping. SMS codes (A) fall to SIM-swap attacks. Security questions (C) are guessable and phishable. Email OTPs (D) are phishable and depend on email account security.

q: A company wants to prove to customers that its release artifacts were built by its trusted CI pipeline from reviewed source code, with no tampering. Which supply-chain control provides this?
options: Code obfuscation
SLSA provenance attestations verifying the build
Unsigned builds are acceptable internally
SBOM alone proves build integrity
explain: SLSA provenance attestations (C) cryptographically record how an artifact was built — source, builder, and steps — so consumers can verify build integrity before deploying. An SBOM (A) lists components but does not prove how the artifact was built. Unsigned builds (B) offer no verification. Obfuscation (D) hides code but proves nothing about the build.
